utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Please be seated. May we hear the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the appearances as far as we can see anybody there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Nicholas Koumjian, Ann Sutherland, and Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Thank you. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic, John Ostojic, and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I hope, Mr. Lukic, you feel better than your voice sounds today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Anything to be discussed beforehand? No, then please, bring the witness, the expert, into the courtroom. It was yesterday in the afternoon that it was confirmed that not only on Monday, Mr. Stanar will arrive, but also Mr. Kuruzovic can be heard as of Wednesday next week. If the parties could please be so kind and think about the question based on our experience whether it would be appropriate to continue with the hearing next Friday. Next Friday originally was a day off. We had no schedule for this day. But especially under the prevailing circumstances and maybe problems with the international air traffic, I would hear submissions by the parties on whether it's possible to sit on Friday next week as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But let's concentrate now on General Wilmot. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You're prepared to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Koumjian, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Koumjian: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when we finished, I was trying to articulate a question about the Hambarine incident. Would it be correct that given that the information that was available was that there was a shootout as you mention in your report.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that as Dr. Mujadzic said, one Muslim was shot, and the people in the car were shot, including two Serbs were killed. Would it be appropriate to investigate to see what exactly had happened and what the sequence of events was in order to determine whether the people at the checkpoint were justified in shooting in self-defence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, such action might be appropriate, to conduct an investigation and see where to go from that point. On the other hand, there was chaos and confusion in the area, and the military had lost at least one person at that event, and so they apparently decided to press on and to go further than -- and could go beyond an investigation and take action immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the Hambarine incident, you mentioned three attacks that happened in Prijedor, and you talked about a period of calm preceding those. But actually the Hambarine incident was not the first shedding of blood in Prijedor, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps to speed things up, could the witness be shown S345.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'll try to avoid questions that are somewhat rhetorical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, S345 is a combat report. If the first page could be put on the ELMO, please, so that everyone can see. And I'm focussing on the very bottom of the first page. The report is dated the 3rd of May, and it indicates on the bottom "In Prijedor, the uncle of the murdered conscript Radenko Dzap killed two and seriously wounded two Muslims. The motive for the killings was revenge." This wasn't mentioned in your report, but in fact this would indicate that what would appear to be an ethnically-based murder, two Muslims killed and three wounded, had taken place shortly after the takeover. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the report indicates, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, before the military conducted operations in Hambarine and Kozarac, there were many orders for disarmament. That was a topic of discussions and negotiations in fact, between the two sides. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, we looked at S28.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown S60, S6-0, and at the same time S389 and S152, to speed things up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, we saw that on the -- sorry. Just to remind us that yesterday we saw on S28, that was the meetings of the 5th of May, that there was a point regarding disarmament, point number 7. I'm now showing you the meetings of the 15th of May of the Council for National Defence of Prijedor Municipal Assembly. And if you look -- if you can just put the first page on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: S60. S6-0, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The next page, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, again this is a meeting attended by Dr. Stakic and representatives of the 43rd Brigade, Vladimir Arsic, commander of the 22nd -- or the Kozara light brigade; Pero Colic; and Slobodan Kuruzovic, the TO commander. Do you see that point number 4 of the discussions of the National Defence Council was the disarmament of paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we look at S389 which we had read one of the articles regarding the Hambarine announcement and the discussions regarding the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To avoid duplications, you can see point 5 of the agenda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Taking over the duties of the military department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What would be your comments on this? Would it be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was an agenda item apparently. I certainly don't know that the duties of the military department were taken over, and in fact disarmament of paramilitary formations was also only an agenda item as listed here. And I note that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please feel free to look on the following pages covering point 4 and point 5. If the usher could please put it on the ELMO in a way that we can read it. You can see the conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you slide it a little bit so we can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And then please, on the next page, AD 5.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it certainly looks like a major endeavour, and what did it say about the press on -- the media on the previous page? Can you put that back up, please. Slide it up a little bit. Slide it up some more. And "with the assistance of the media, the public security station Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in concert with the army's command should draft the plan of disarmament after which the actual process should be set in motion and with the assistance of the media." I really don't understand what we're talking about, how does the media play into this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in your experience in dictatorships, is it common for the government to control the media and to use the media to control the population?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and certainly the media could be used as a propaganda tool. And so if that's what the inference is, then I can understand it from that standpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Going to S389, sir, we read S389-1A yesterday regarding the demands on Hambarine. These, sir, are announcements that appeared in an issue of a local newspaper. I'm now turning to page 2, please, S389-2. I'm just going to read selected paragraphs of this document, and if you would like me to add anything, please feel free. In the middle of the second article, S389-2A, the middle paragraph -- the witness should be shown the translation. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We don't have an English translation, it was on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It was handed out. I'm sorry. It's S389-2A. Ms. Karper indicates it was just handed out Friday. I'm sorry. If we don't have it now, I could move on to another... The second page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in the middle paragraph of this article dated the 23rd of May, it indicates "the Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff hereby revokes the decision on the deadline for the surrender of weapons by 1500 hours on 27 May" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will you slow down please, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The Crisis Staff orders immediate and unconditional surrender of weapons and military equipment. At the collection point set up in Zarko Zgonjanin barracks by 1800 hours today, 23 May, the latest." Moving on to the next article, but on the same page, the last paragraph, it indicates: "The Crisis Staff and the regional command shall see the operation of disarming paramilitary formations through to the end. There has been a strong warning that the order to remove blocks from all roads in the area of Prijedor Municipality must be carried out, particularly from the section of the Prijedor/Banja Luka Highway between the local communities of Kozarusa and Omarska." Sir, this article was also dated the -- this announcement, the 24th of May. Would it be correct, then, to say that any military commander in that area would have been aware of roadblocks in the Kozarac area, would have been aware that the people in Kozarac were not willing to surrender their weapons, and were opposing the occupation of Kozarac by the forces aligned with the SDS government, and would expect there to be combat if they tried to move in and occupy Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I would object to the form of the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Some reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Specifically with respect to the word "occupation."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If Mr. Ostojic suggests another word, I'll use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not here to suggest anything for counsel, but it's inappropriate in light of the evidence that we heard over the course of the last 11 months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The final assessment of course will be with the Bench, but if you could use another term.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps the General could help me. When you take over territory and control it, what word do you use in the military?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you take over territory and control it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you take over territory from a population that's against your force --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's opposed to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you call that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're occupying it, I would say. So the question is, sir? I've lost myself here in the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you're really testing me. The question was that: Given the situation that existed at the time, public announcements, clear public knowledge that there were -- there was opposition to the occupation that the people of Kozarac had erected some type of defence and roadblocks, that a military commander would expect if you drive military vehicles or troops towards Kozarac, would expect combat?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Same objection, Your Honour. If the Court would like, I can expand on it. Quite candidly, I believe the evidence, with all due respect, doesn't show that there was occupation in Kozarac. The people in Kozarac were specifically those people who set up the blockades initially, as were defined throughout the witnesses, both the Prosecution witnesses and the Defence witnesses. To imply that there was an occupation by other forces, namely from the SDS, as the question clearly indicates, is erroneous and is misleading and it's suggesting facts that are not in evidence at all. So I think it's distorted. The question could be placed, if I may suggest, that the people within Kozarac who were maintaining positions there while they were armed, should a military convoy pass through an armed checkpoint that they may perceive to be hostile.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, I'll accept that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you answer Mr. Ostojic's suggested form of the question.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military was in the area. There was a faction of people in that area that didn't want the military there. They apparently set up checkpoints. They apparently set up roadblocks on occasion. When the military commander moved through there, he should have recognised that there was a threat there against his forces, and therefore he could expect trouble. He might expect trouble. He might take certain precautions to ensure that his troops were safe, and he might be ready also to respond in the event that he was brought under attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, sir, wouldn't it make more sense, from what you know about the events, that it wasn't a convoy passing through Kozarac that was attacked, but there was an attack on Kozarac that was resisted?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll object to the form of the question, Your Honour, again, and I would ask the Court to look at the report by the OTP's military analyst specifically who gives a definition as to what occurred, and that's inconsistent clearly on its face and all fours with their own expert's view of the events in his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: At this late stage of the procedure, it's extremely difficult to intervene for a Chamber. But on the other hand, I think it's the right for each party to articulate the own opinion and to put the case to the witness, may it be supported by evidence or not. It's just to put the case to the witness. And I think it's not misleading at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I can just, Your Honour, I agree that they should put the case in front of the witness. But the Defence is thinking the case is what their witnesses have said the case is. So if they have called a military analyst who works for the OTP and has articulated a certain position, that's what the case should --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. We don't want to have closing arguments right now. Would Mr. Koumjian please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, as a military commander, would you send a -- your forces to drive through areas occupied by a hostile enemy without -- and not expect them to come under attack?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would depend upon the formation that I sent through that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. so-called hostile area. If I was involved in a show of force, I would send a military organisation that was sizable, that was well-armed, and then I might not expect an attack at all. So it has a lot to do with how that force was presented as it went through that so-called threatened area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like the witness to look at a few pages of transcript, and so everyone has copies, I can hand them out. We have some for the booth. Perhaps we have one copy for the B/C/S booth, and I'll try to read slowly. I believe it starts with the testimony of Mr. Jusuf Arifagic on page 7.123 of our trial transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You'll see that he was asked: "Are you aware of a request issued by the Banja Luka command concerning a passage of a military convoy on the 24th of May, 1992, when the conflict in Kozarac broke out?" Answer: "I am not." Question: "But you must be aware of the fact that on that day, there was a convoy of military vehicles moving from the direction of Banja Luka?" Answer: "Yes, I heard that." Question from Mr. Lukic: "You heard when Kapetan Cirkin was being briefed by a local checkpoint there, that is the checkpoint from Jakupovici, who was telling him that a military convoy was approaching?" Answer: "Yes." Question: "You also heard when Kapetan Cirkin issued commands to the person who had called him from that checkpoint, that is, when he told him that he shall let the tanks come close to him, close enough so that he could destroy them with a hand-held rocket launcher, with a Zolja?" Answer: "Yes, but the convoy did not consist only of" -- Answer: "Yes, but the convoy did not consist only of tanks but also of infantry troops. It was not an ordinary military convoy moving along a road; it was a classical military attack." Question: "Do" you know that at least one of the tanks was destroyed?" "Yes, I think that's what I heard subsequently, that one was destroyed and that one was put out of order. Whether this information is accurate, I don't know, I was not there." Sir, another witness testified who had been a high-school student at the time, and that is Sanja Poljak. On page 6.328 of the trial transcript, beginning on line 23, he said: "I remember clearly around 1.00 in the afternoon, I was sitting in my house. I was having lunch. On the table we had a radio set, tape recorder -- how should I say it? I was listening to Radio Prijedor. At that time, they had news on the radio, and they carried a piece of news which really scared me in a way. They said that unless the barricades were removed from the Banja Luka/Prijedor main road, Kozarac and the surrounding areas would be attacked." Going to page 6.333, Mr. Poljak's testimony, he was asked on line 10: "I want to stop and go back and ask you some questions about what you've just told us. You said that shooting started and shelling. Can you describe to us exactly what you heard and saw." Answer: "That was -- how should I put it? Suddenly the shooting came, and then shells started falling. The shelling began. You had the impression they were coming from all possible directions. They fell on fields and on houses. It all happened at once." "So you heard the sounds of shooting and then the shelling began?" "I don't think the shelling stopped before Wednesday. Shells were falling all the time." Question: "We're now talking about the 24th of May and do you remember what day of the week that was? Answer: "Sunday." Question: "When you say that shells were coming and falling everywhere, how much time was there between on average to your best estimate between when you would hear the explosions of these shells?" Answer: "Well, every two or three minutes, I don't know exactly. I just know that shells were falling all the time." Question: "What was being shelled? Did it seem to you that any particular area was being targeted? What was there to be hit?" Answer: "They targeted everything. Even when we started to run across the fields. There were no houses there but still also those areas were being shelled, the forest too. Maybe they were watching us with binoculars, but they were shelling all the areas. I had the impression that shells were falling literally all over the place, so we retreated slowly, and as soon as we heard a shell whistle by, we would just run for shelter." And then Mr. Poljak was asked on page 66 -- 6.334, the very bottom line, 25 -- well, excuse me, 23: "Did anyone who was present at the barricade tell you at any time what happened there?" Answer: "When we were retreating, we reached a forest. We paused to get some rest. There was a creek there and the place was quite sheltered, and my cousin told me there what had happened." Question: "What did he tell you happened at the checkpoint?" Answer: "They were there, and suddenly a tank drove up from the direction of Omarska. And in the spot where the barricade was, perhaps 2 or 300 metres from there, there was a creek and a forest. And as the tank drove across the bridge, it was followed by a group of soldiers who then lined up beside the tank and they started shooting, the shooting began." "Did your cousin tell you whether the people at the checkpoint or barricade fired back at the tank or at the soldiers that were coming from Omarska?" Answer: "Yes, they did fire back a bit, and then they fled." Sir, to avoid -- let me first ask you, sir, would it be a classical attack formation to approach a point where forces are deployed, dug in, by having tanks flanked by infantry?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that could be a formation that was used. I note that the first -- the first witness said something about yes, but the convoy did not consist only of tanks, but also of infantry troops. It was not an ordinary military convoy moving along a road. It was a classical military attack. Convoys can move along the road with tanks and armoured personnel carriers and troops and supply trucks and all sorts of vehicles, and it's still a convoy. So I'm not sure that I understand what the witness is talking about here. But in answer to your question, yes, an attack on a point can consist of a combination of armour and infantry working in league with each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I want to talk to you a little bit about the balance of forces that existed at the time. Is it correct that there was not a balance of forces, that there was overwhelming force in favour of the VRS/SDS side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I've read, it sounded like there were about a thousand to 1200 what we called or what someone called red berets in that particular area. There were apparently foot soldiers. They were apparently -- maybe even soldiers that operated as guerillas at night and in terrorist activities and so on and so forth. So if you're asking me if there was an imbalancer between the tank and that soldier of the berets, I guess there is. But a military commander doesn't choose up sides here and say, Well, look they have got a bunch of infantry soldiers over there, so I can only use infantry soldiers over here --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's perfectly understood. That's not my question. I understand there's no obligation to balance your force to the enemy's.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No there isn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that's understood.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was out of balance, but there was no obligation to balance it. Besides, this is a command decision. It's a military decision. It's in the stove pipe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a -- despite the fact that you read that this was ordered by the Crisis Staff according to the announcements in the newspaper, that is still your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure it was ordered by the Crisis Staff. You say that the media was the tool, one of the tools of that particular government. So I can see that that tool was used, maybe someone else made a decision like a commander, and he only asked that Crisis Staff to make sure that the population knew it by putting it out in the media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it change your opinion if you heard that Dr. Stakic made a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. statement that this was a -- that we decided to attack Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: So now he is involved in the decision-making of the military? He may have said that, but I doubt that he's the one that concluded the attack plan, developed the forces that would go in, created the formations, devised the tactics and the techniques. I don't think he did that. I don't think he could do that. I don't think he would be authorised to do that, and I don't think the military would even talk to him about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's clear, sir. There's no allegation that he was a tactician. The question is whether or not he influenced the military and effected that attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So I would ask the usher to please hand out S187.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, may I respond to that last comment?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the principle of unity of command, I don't think that he would influence a military at all. It was probably a military decision if such an attack was conducted, because after all, they have limited resources and they make choices. So I don't think Dr. Stakic could say to them, attack over here in zone A and forgot about zone B. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, who does tell the military what to do? When the military attacks citizens of its own country, are you saying they do that on completely their own decision or do they follow political --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they take a look at the threat in the area. They take a look at the intelligence, and they make decisions based on that. Those intelligence reports go up and down the chain of command, and some higher authority in the military decides we're going to go here and do something about this situation here. I just don't think it takes place from outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Broadly if -- sorry. Broadly if I could interrupt, would it be correct that it's the political leadership that would set such goals as where the borders of this new state would be, whether it would have access to the sea, strategic goals such as that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I imagine that strategic goals such as that are the purview of the political arm of the country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The military would carry out those strategic goals, it would be their job to fulfill those goals correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could very well be if there were military implications associated with those goals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If one of those goals was the separation of nationalities, it would be the military's responsibility, if that was so ordered by the political leadership, to carry that out?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that was one of the goals, and I certainly haven't taken a look at what the goals may have been, but yes, that could be true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, on page 6 of 187, S187, this is a transcript of an interview with Dr. Stakic. And at the bottom, the last question by the reporter was: "On the way here, we drove past Kozarac. And from what we know, there was a big battle in Kozarac. What happened there?" Dr. Stakic: "That is precisely where that Muslim extremism escalated because Kozarac, with its surroundings, had around 20.000 Muslims. And in Kozarac itself, which has 10 to 12.000, we found original lists with 3 and a half thousand, or to be precise, 3.791 members of the illegal Muslim Territorial Defence, the number of each gun, and the date on which it was issued, and other light and medium heavy weapons. We had indications that this existed before; however, the fact and the moment when they came out to the Prijedor/Banja Luka main road and blocked around 10 kilometres of it at the entrance to and exit from their territory, and all local access roads, the army -- actually, we made a decision that the army and police go up there and lift the blockade of that road." Is it still your position that Dr. Stakic could have had no influence on that decision?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: He might have influenced the decision, but it looks to me like there must have been some sort of threat evaluation also conducted which allowed the commander to make the ultimate decision and to take the action. I still don't think that Dr. Stakic said, "Commander, go do that."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, does this brief excerpt that I read also indicate that Dr. Stakic apparently had detailed briefings about the results of the combat operations and that he lists the exact number of members of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that materials flowed back and forth into his organisation which he probably read, and I'm sure that being resident in the area, he had some idea of the statistics and the demographics of the area. So I presume that he was quite familiar with what was taking place in the region where he lived, in his neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, on footnote 91 of your report, you quote Witness P. And on line 15, beginning on line 12, he's asked about guns in the possession of the Territorial Defence. I'll give you time to find that. That was footnote 91 of your report.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he answered: "Well, a number of rifles had been bought from the Serb reservist coming back from Croatia and from the battlefield there and sold rifles to the local population. What the ratio between the received and purchased rifles are, I do not know. I cannot tell you. The only thing I do know and I heard about was that there was about 400 rifles. And how many automatic, how many semi-automatic, I do not know. As far as ammunition is concerned, well, some amount was mentioned, but the policeman said, 'Well, we can defend ourselves for five minutes, and then we're finished.'" And then, sir, there's also a report, footnote 75 of your report, which is a report from the Prijedor public security station dated the 5th of July. And point number 7 indicates the weapons and ammunition seized. 16 automatic rifles, 7 M48, 184 hunting rifles, 24 hunting carbines, some pistols and MK rifles. What I'm really interested in are the last two items on the next page, pistol ammunition, 540; hunting ammunition, 500. Sir, does it appear to you that the defenders of Kozarac had very little ammunition at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this expose, they have very little ammunition, but who knows what they have behind it? I think it's a very limited report. 540 rounds of ammunition when properly used can take out 540 people, so I can take that position as easily as the position that you've taken on this point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, would it make sense if you were a commander of those forces, would you expect to be able to attack and defeat the JNA/VRS forces that were in the area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Attack and defeat the JNA forces in the area, probably not. But you could certainly disrupt, cause chaos and confusion, reduce the economic situation in the area to absolute -- a nothing, ruin the -- just completely distract everybody from normal life. So this kind of conflict in this situation is one in which a conventional force is probably -- is probably not the force to be countering the organisation that's there. But that's what was available, so they used the conventional force to do so. It's a very difficult situation, there's no doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the -- I want to take advantage of your expertise in weapons, which I don't have. A Winchester rifle, can you explain to the Court what that is.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody named Winchester built a rifle, and I'm not sure exactly which rifle we're talking about now. Maybe it's a 30-calibre rifle, possibly it's as a rifle that you use if you're a hunter, and I'm not a hunter. Possibly you use that kind of rifle to bag a deer or animals of that size for consumption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, as a former intelligence officer, if you received information, and just for counsel and the Court, I'm referring to S162-5, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the newspaper article about the arrest of Becir Medunjanin, that the commander of the Territorial Defence in Kozarac was arrested with a Winchester rifle, would that suggest to you as a military intelligence officer that additional evidence that the defenders were very poorly armed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it would suggest anything to me. If you came into my house in Sedona Arizona and arrested me today, you would find a 45-calibre pistol. And I don't think that any intelligence officer could make anything out of that. I don't see it as significant, and as an intelligence officer, I wouldn't make any evaluation of the fact that the gentleman had on his person or in his home, wherever he was arrested, a Winchester rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown S350, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, again, taking advantage of your experience and I give credit to the Court - I'm about to plagiarise a question that was asked of Mr. Brown by one of the Judges, Judge Vassylenko, can you, sir, explain to us -- you don't have to refer to the article right now. This question is a little separate. As a military expert, in a situation where there are people defending territory and dug in, they have chosen the ground, they have had time to build fortifications and to dig in, and you are the attacker, would it be correct that normally we would assume much greater casualties on the side of the attacking force than on the side of the dug-in defenders who are -- who have chosen the ground?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Interesting question. And it very much depends upon the ratio, the combat power ratio between the defender and the attacker. Conventional wisdom says it takes a ratio of about 3 to 1 to successfully succeed in an attack. Now, if the commander that's attacking has the capability to prepare the defensive positions in that he can conduct artillery and air strikes against those positions, then move tanks forward, move his artillery forward to continue the attack, move his infantry in, I don't think that the defender would necessarily have the advantage. It all depends on the formations. It depends on the tactics. It depends upon the fire power of the attacking force.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Looking now at S350, it's a combat report.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that this one, sir?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Of the 1st Krajina Corps, and it's regarding the destruction of the Green Beret in the wider area of Kozarac. You see under point number 4 that it indicates that in the wider area of Kozarac village, then lists the villages, Kozarusa, Trnopolje, Donja Jakupovici, Gornji Jakupovici, Benkovac, Ratkovic, that these areas had been entirely freed of Green Berets, 80 to 100 Green Berets were killed, and about 1500 captured. It indicates our own casualties are five killed and 20 wounded, and minor damage already repaired on the track assembly of two M84 tanks. Sir, as a military intelligence officer, would this results -- knowing what you know about the attack on Kozarac, would these results, 80 to a hundred Green Berets killed and only 5 of the attacking force killed, suggest that perhaps these Green Berets were killed after being taken into custody, after surrendering?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Object to the form of the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Some reason, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, if counsel could state which witness claimed this hypothetical that is not only purely speculative but it just an attempt on his part to distort the evidence, their witnesses not one of them have suggested dispute the fact that many of their witnesses were actually in and around the Kozarac area at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, no evaluation of evidence at this point in time. May the witness be asked on the basis of the document we have before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: My objection on the basis would be speculation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When we have a document before us, I don't think it's speculation. When the question is just based on this, and once again, please, may I ask both parties to refrain from starting an attempt to anticipate the closing arguments.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me take a shot at your question. As a military intelligence officer, would this, knowing what you know about the attack in Kozarac, would these results 80 a hundred Green Berets killed and only 5 in the attacking force killed suggest that perhaps the Green Berets were killed after being taken into custody after surrendering. Well, not necessarily so. Because in earlier questioning, you pointed out to me the heavy concentrations of artillery fire in the area, and artillery shells were falling everywhere and coming from every direction, is what your question said or what the witness stated. And so it seems to me that some of that firing could have been very much targeted against the Green Berets, and certainly 80 Green Berets could have been killed in that kind of an attack. I guess the point you're trying to make, but there were only 5 killed on the other side. Well, we also talked about the imbalance of fire power and capability between the JNA and the Green Berets. So I would assume that the JNA, being in some ways and in some cases an armoured force, offered more protection to its soldiers because it was armoured, and therefore its casualties would normally be less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, somewhat in response to Mr. Ostojic's request, there was a Witness B that testified in this case. If as a military intelligence officer, if you discovered the bodies, and I cannot quote the number, I'm looking for the transcript, but of a group - I'm sure it was more than six - individuals in police uniform lying in a parking lot, shot dead, would that suggest to you an execution?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it certainly could, especially if they were all lined up in a row as if they had been collected or they had been organised so that they could be assassinated, and they fell right where they were assassinated. That would certainly suggest an execution to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you mentioned, and you correctly stated, that under the laws of war, those people involved in hostilities, defenders, can be taken to camps, can be detained during the conflict. Sir, there's testimony in this case that the defender of the -- the commander of the Territorial Defence in Kozarac, Becir Medunjanin, was taken to Omarska, the commander of the attack on Prijedor the 30th of May, Slavko Ecimovic was taken to the camps, and both of these individuals were tortured and killed. Is that within the laws of war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Prisoners are to be treated fairly. And they are not to be tortured. They are not to be killed. They are not to be raped. They are not to be beaten. And so that is absolutely contrary to the rules of the Geneva Convention. And those people who are responsible for that should have been investigated and action taken against them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we leave the Document S350 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, just one question. Who would have to take action and to report to which body? What would be the role of the military court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in this case, it would certainly be within the confines of the military. At least from everything I've read, it looks as if the military established, operated, maintained, and administered these camps. They did have some assistance apparently from the police. But it would in my view fall on the military that such investigations and follow-up would be their responsibility. One can say, well, they were the ones that perpetrated those acts in the camp. They did. But somehow, they must have been uncovered. They are being presented here in this case, and follow-up action on those people should have been the result.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree that whoever it was that established the camps and made decisions to detain people would have a responsibility for ensuring the safety of those individuals?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. Administer, maintain, and operate are the operative words here, I think. Establishing the camp is simply selecting the piece of ground where the camp could be set up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm talking about a decision, when I say establish a camp, to detain individuals, to put them into a place, to keep them there against their will. If you decide to put someone into that custody, aren't you responsible that they are treated humanely and that they are not killed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask to pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Continue, General. THE WINTESS: Yes, I'm just rereading the question again. I still take the position that it is the role of the military to ensure that these people are treated humanely. The establishment of the camp, that's a minor decision, and it involves facilities. It involves somebody saying you can use those 12 buildings over there that have a fence around them and open up a camp or facility. But it's the people that are there, it's the people that are on site, it's the people that are in the daily business of policing, securing, administering the detainees in that camp that are responsible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, I'm sorry. Before leaving S350, the document in front of you, if you could look at point number 2, do you see that it indicates the forces that were at the disposal of the attacking force and that participated in the conflict? It says: "Components of the 343rd Motorised Brigade, an enlarged motorised battalion, supported by two 105-millimetre Howitzer batteries and one M84 tank squadron." Would you say that this force was overwhelming stronger than the information you have about the defending force?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say that it was overwhelmingly stronger than the defending force. I would also say that every prudent commander goes with all that he's got. He takes everything he's got.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's understood. Sir -- just to correct the record, I said Witness B as in boy, it should be "P" as in Paul, page 337, where the witness to testified to seeing at least ten bodies. Sir, if these are prisoner of war camps, you do not detain civilians. Correct? Civilians, those people not taking part in the hostilities cannot be detained as prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a general rule, you certainly don't detain civilians. But in some circumstances, you're forced to do that. Because you've got to sort out who is a civilian and who is the person who is causing the problem, doing things at night that you don't want them to do. So you may have to detain a whole large group of people, you may have to move them to a camp and interrogate them to sort out who they are and what they are doing and why they were in that region or that location. It could turn out very well that they were simply people who lived there and they were caught up in the combat situation. But you have to figure that out, and the only way to figure it out may be to detain them, to ask them questions, and to see how they fit into the greater picture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, would you detain -- are you justified in detaining those who are participating in Gandhian-like resistance, nonviolent resistance, political resistance?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably as a general course, general course of events, Gandhian-like resistance, absolutely peaceful resistance, I would say probably not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going to your stove pipe analysis for a moment -- excuse me, let me stay on the subject of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown S238.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you establish a prisoner of war camp, you are required to allow the International Red Cross to visit. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Every military makes sure that their commanders understand that. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's normally very much part of a training programme.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: S238A is a newspaper article from the local newspaper Kozarski Vjesnik dated the 27th of July, 1992, regarding a visit from leaders of the regional Crisis Staff and other individuals from Banja Luka, the chief of the regional police, to Prijedor. And I'm interested in the quote on the last page. Apparently at this meeting, it indicates -- first before I -- that there was present Vladimir Arsic, Milomir Stakic, and Simo Drljaca, among others. And Predrag Radic, who was the president of the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka, spoke about the significance of events in Prijedor and his views concerning Banja Luka. And I'm interested in the very last four lines where he says: "The International Red Cross has been trying for days to reach Prijedor. But as we have stated, we will make it possible for them only after they have personally acknowledged the situation of Serbian refugees and captives in Odzak, Rascani, Travnik, Zenica, Sarajevo, Konjic, and many other places." Sir, is it proper to prohibit the International Red Cross to visit POW camps because you want them to first go see the camps on the other side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, no, it's not -- it is not good form to prevent the Red Cross from visiting camps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, one of the -- I may have to come back later to this.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have it. I have a new document, if it could be distributed. It has the ERN number 00848550. It's one of the documents cited in Mr. Brown's report and previously disclosed but not exhibited, not given an exhibit number. Sir, this document is dated the 3rd of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't know if Your Honour wants to give it a number now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Immediately, this would be S426. Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this is an order from General Talic, the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, which included the region of Prijedor dated the 3rd of August, 1992, in which he indicates that he's received verbally an order from the main staff commander that a visit by an international committee and a team of reporters to the detention camps in Manjaca, Trnopolje, Omarska, and Prijedor had been approved to take place within the next two days. Would this indicate to you that the command of these camps had knowledge that the foreign journalists were going to visit on the 5th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how did you arrive at the date the 5th of August? Did I miss something here?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, there's testimony that that is the date of the visit, and this order dated the 3rd of August indicates "within two days."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it appears as if the appropriate personnel have been notified and it's -- it appears to be within the military chain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first sentence of the second paragraph says: "In this regard, all measures are to be taken to make conditions in these camps satisfactory." Sir, the conditions in the camps by law should have been satisfactory before people were detained there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way, sir, do you know the difference between the Manjaca camp and the Omarska and Keraterm camps and how they were structured and who was running the camp?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The details of who was running the camps by name, no, I don't know. But I believe in the documentation that I looked at, it appeared to be military people running the camps, and they seemed to be the ones that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were in charge. And there were some instances where they were assisted by elements of the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Moving back to your stove pipe analysis and the chain of command, fundamental to that, as I understand it, is that an officer follows the orders of his superior in the military and is not influenced by politicians or political factors in the area. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your report, you footnoted, footnote 81, an interview with Radmilo Zeljaja, and I'd like you to please take a look at that document. And specifically, if you could look to the page that's stamped at the bottom 00332748.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could that be put on the ELMO. I don't know if Your Honours all have a copy of that. Perhaps it could be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, at the top of that page that begins -- that's stamped 2748.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's stamped at the bottom 2748 as an ERN number. I think this document also has an S number. 274. Excuse me, S274. So perhaps we should use that. I'm sorry. Sir, in this interview, Colonel Radmilo Zeljaja says -- states: "It is true. The brigade command was, because of that, immediately linked to the leadership of the SDS giving them important support, as they do for all decent Serbs, to organise themselves for self-defence in case of an attack by the Muslims forces. As to the security and intelligence at that time, we cover this entire region in order to gather information about SDA involvement, its activities, plans, et cetera. Precisely at those turbulent political times of the dissolution of Yugoslavia and the JNA, some of its units joined the army of the then Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina. Surely, we considered all those options then in the command and army headquarters. And I can say here for the first time that we were forced to keep quiet and not to carry out certain orders by our headquarters, which is not typical for soldiers. One of these orders was to move technical equipment, weapons, and the brigade from this region to Serbia." So, sir, would this indicate to you that the chain of command had been breached in the 43rd Motorised Brigade, and that Radmilo Zeljaja and the headquarters of that brigade were influenced by political issues and political leadership, and not simply following commands?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not clear to me. It says that because of that immediate link to the leadership of the Serb Democratic Party, giving them important support as they do for all decent Serbs, I don't know if we're talking about actual support, if we're talking about we're going to be your cheerleaders, let's stay in touch. I'm not sure what it means. And then I guess your other point is, farther down, about not accepting orders. "We were forced to keep quiet and not to carry out certain orders of our headquarters," which is not typical for soldiers. "One of these orders was to move technical equipment, weapons, and the brigade from the region of Serbia."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why don't you please read the next sentence also.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I repeat that I am saying this for the first time. It may cost me." Who knows. "We burnt that telegram as we were ready, especially Colonel Arsic, at that time, he was the commander of the brigade and I was the chief of staff. We knew that from the day of mobilisation onwards, we would lead the people. We would look into battle until the very end. The fight for the goals that we are fighting for now, we have never given up these goals, and this is the creation of a Serbian state in these areas." It sounds as if in these troubled times that there were certain members of the Serbian democratic party that influenced the military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, would you say that the smoke was coming out of the side of the stove pipe at that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The smoke in that instance may have been coming out of the side of the stove pipe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you turn to the next page -- sorry I hope you have it out. In the first full paragraph, I'm going to go to the middle, and I'll read it out. You can follow with me. "We did not manage to establish any normal relations at all with the SDA, the party, that was then in power. Of course, we then offered maximal help and support to the SDS, both in organising preparations and advising them, in order to overcome certain problems and to take power. The role of the militia is undeniable here, the role of Mr. Drljaca and Mr. Jankovic, who carried out the orders directly. I must emphasise here in this region, and more or less everyone knows that, the very close cooperation between the army and police. Such cooperation was also established with the leaders of the party, and the people in power, the Crisis Staff, and all decent Serbs who were and still are of importance for this town." Sir, does it sound to you that the military leadership of the 43rd Brigade was very closely linked to the police and the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from my cooperative standpoint, yes, they were very linked. So "cooperation" is the key word here. And I don't find that unusual. If, for example, the military needs housing for its soldiers coming into town, they might very well visit with the city officials and arrange to use a school gymnasium to house the troops overnight. That's cooperation. So the word "cooperation" is used, and I can see and understand that that could be a very normal process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can the civilian leadership influence personnel decisions, promotions, or the hiring or firing of military officers, the positions that they hold?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my experience, they don't. I would think it would be very disruptive to the military officer who is in the military. He would ask himself, well, who do I work for?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown S392, D51, S26, and S27. I'll start with S392, please. If that could be put on the ELMO, because I don't think everyone has a copy, the first page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: S392 is a -- it's marked "Military Secret, Confidential," dated the 9th of June, 1992. And entitled "Report on the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff Decision." And sir, I think it's understood in this Court that that's a civilian body. It indicates: "One of the issues that was discussed at yesterday's session of the autonomous region Bosnian Krajina Crisis Staff was the general personnel policy in the army of the 1st Krajina Corps." Going down a sentence: "An ultimatum was issued" -- let me read it. "It was stated that within the units of the 1st Krajina Corps, the 14th logistics base, and the units of the air force and anti-aircraft defence in Banja Luka garrison, there were 67 officers of Muslim or Croatian nationality. An ultimatum was issued requesting removal of these persons from vital and command posts by 15 June, 1992, or they will take control over the armed forces. We consider their demand to be justified, but it is impossible to find adequate professional replacements among the reserve staff and active officers of Bosnian origin -- originating from Bosnia-Herzegovina, are not arriving from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." Then, if we look, sir, at D51, a subsequent report dated 13th June, it indicates halfway down in paragraph 6, on the second page, paragraph 6, "the purging of officers on an ethnic basis remains a topic of discussion because of the danger that it may very soon result in deficiencies in the units, but it is proceeding in the spirit of the order received." And, sir, if you could look at a couple documents related specifically to Prijedor, S26, indicates -- dated the 5th of May: "Eso Bucan is hereby dismissed from the post of commander for logistics security effective as of 5th of May, 1992. This decision shall take effect on the day of its adoption, and Major Radmilo Zeljaja shall see to its implementation." S27 is the next document. This indicates that Vahid Ceric is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. hereby dismissed from the post of assistant commander for the organisation of mobilisation and personnel affairs as of the 5th of May. And again, Zeljaja is responsible for implementation. Sir, does it appear to you that in the spring, summer of 1992, personnel decisions of the newly-formed Serbian army were influenced by political leadership in Prijedor and the ARK region.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Object to the form of the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think the witness may be asked to comment on these documents and what it says. And there needs no other comment on this. The documents have a language, and it's for the witness to explain what he can read from these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The question is put in the form that's inappropriate, because he first cites Exhibit 392, and then follows from his question a presumption that 392 precedes the other two documents. So it's inappropriate in all its sense to the form. You can't have something that happened subsequent, and then ask him, was this based on this directive which happened one month later? It's simply not only illogical, but it's inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think the General has all the powers to read and to follow the rules of logic. So please, answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who did the document go to, first of all? Who is it addressed to? It's a decision statement. It's that "I've decided" signed by the president of. Is it an action item? Did it go here? Were these actions taken? Were the results apparent? Did these people lose their jobs? I don't know. All I see is a decision paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see that it's copied to the individual involved and Major Radmilo Zeljaja.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about S27 and S26.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do see that. Did they lose their jobs as a result of that action?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you're saying that did they lose their jobs as a result of that action, you would agree that the political leadership had very significant influence in that it could determine personnel, promotions, and positions within the brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess my problem is that I don't understand how this --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Again, I object to the form of the question. I could explain it, Your Honour, because I think it's not a deliberate attempt, but these members, if Mr. Koumjian can establish were members of the brigade or of the TO at that time, so it's significant whether they were part of the civilian at that time on May 5th or were they part of the military at that time, which ultimately after May 12th as the Court very well knows was incorporated and was disbanded after May 20th. I mean, it's relatively clear. These are significant events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's not objecting to the form. That's an argument which counsel can make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Absolutely. And I really, for the third time, I ask now explicitly the Defence, please refrain from anticipating closing arguments. There is nothing -- even following your words, your own words, there is nothing what one could regard as an objection to the form of the question. So therefore, please answer the question, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it appears as if they did have influence over the personnel situation as it existed in the army. I wonder if, however, in the final analysis, it's a legal order? I mean, what happened here to the military chain of command? How can all of a sudden a civilian fire you from the army if he is not even in the army to begin with? So I wonder about this decision and its validity and its legality. So it's a very confusing issue for me, and based on my experience, I've never seen anything like it before. And I can't imagine how we got to this kind of decision, and I can't imagine if it was carried out. It also seems to be somehow associated with earlier events where certain members of the JNA were defecting from that force early on and helping to create a different army. And it seems to me maybe that these people, if they were identified as being part of that group, maybe somehow, there's an association there. So as a military expert, I don't understand how this could possibly work when it's not formalised within the institution called the army, and yet someone here has made a decision and said "you are no longer part of the military." So it's somewhat confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think this is an appropriate point in time --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's about as far as I can go. I just don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We will come back to this, but before we have the break, we have a logistic question. I think based on the long cross-examination, and it will continue, it is only fair to give additional time for the re-examination to the Defence. Therefore, my question, first of all, to you, General, is: What is your actual flight schedule?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My flight schedule is to depart tomorrow morning at 11.30 from Amsterdam to Los Angeles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So you would be available this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any objections by the parties to continue this morning until 12.30. That would allow us to continue in Courtroom I as of 2.00 until 4.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then we will proceed this way. The trial stays adjourned until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. I just learned that we can only start at 2.15, and then continue until 4.45 in Courtroom I this afternoon. Mr. Koumjian, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, General, would you agree that anyone employed is influenced by those people who are paying their salaries?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown S77.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, S77 -- sorry. Perhaps the first page could be put on the ELMO so that all could see it. I see it's there. Sir, this indicates -- this conclusion of the Crisis Staff signed Milomir Stakic dated the 16th of June, 1992, indicates that Simo Drljaca, who was the chief of police as you know; Ranko Travar, who was the secretary for the economy; and Radovan Rajlic are charged with making a comprehensive review of the possibilities and set criteria and recommend to the Crisis Staff the manner of payment to and catering for the army and the police in Prijedor. Would this indicate to you that there was funding by the municipal authorities for at least part of the army and police budgets?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what part of the police budget and the army budget we're speaking of. There's operations and maintenance. There's all sorts of budgets probably divided into separate accounts. So I really don't know if we're talking about personnel payments or what it is we're discussing here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps, then, the witness could be shown S250.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, S250, as it is coming, I'll explain to you, is a document of the decisions passed by the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor confirming decisions of the Crisis Staff during the time when the Crisis Staff was meeting in place of the Municipal Assembly. I'm just going to go through - this is a lengthy document - a few of the decisions, and ask you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. at the end about whether you find them significant. And particularly, sir, I'm interested in whether this affects your view of the influence of the civilian authorities over the army, over the police, and over the detention camps. On the 29th of June -- excuse me, 29th of May, 1992, the enactments passed on that date, decisions 3 and 4, regard dismissing the Serbian Territorial Defence commander, and 4, determining that the Territorial Defence is no longer required. On the 31st of May, the first conclusion, prohibiting the return of POWs to Trnopolje and Prijedor. Going, if you could flip the page two pages over, to the 5th of June, page 3, the first order forbidding unauthorised shooting. The fifth order on procedures by the military police and the public security station. The ninth order, on the forming of a logistics unit. Going to the 6th of June, the fifth order, making Crisis Staff members responsible for providing efficient security for the hospital. The seventh conclusion, on the continuation of the blockade measures. Flipping the page, page 4, going to the very last, the bottom of the page, enactment on the 9th of June, conclusion number 13, making the regional command responsible for transferring equipment from a road company, Kozaraputevi to the collection centre, Orlovaca. Flipping the page, the fifth page, the 10th of June. The first conclusion, requesting the municipal secretariat to report on the logistics base; the second conclusion, assigning the duty of providing security for the Trnopolje camp to the regional command. Going to the 11th of June -- I'll skip that, excuse me. It doesn't relate to the police and army specifically. Flipping the page, page 6, these are first decisions from the 12th of June at the top of the page. Number 5, conclusion on the liberalisation of the procedure for issuing movement permits to citizens; conclusion number 8, concerning the continuing operation of the logistics base in Cirkin Polje and the provision of food for refugees and prisoners. Going to the 16th of June, first conclusion, assigning members of the Crisis Staff the duty of preparing a system of supplying food to the army and police troops. Flipping the page, page 7, the first order concerning the formation of a single intervention platoon. And sir, I don't know -- I believe we could show you the full order, but it concerns a joint intervention platoon made up of members of the military and the police. The fourth order concerning the obligation to report on procurement of military equipment. The 11th -- this is from the 17th of June, the 11th conclusion concerning pay for the reserve police force for the month of April 1992, specifically answering your question about whether that concerned pay. Going to the 23rd of June, the 6th conclusion on page 8, directed to the regional command to ensure uniformity of Serbian army insignia. The 22nd of June, the third conclusion, responsibility for collecting refugees from Cela, Donja Puharska, and Trnopolje. Flipping the page, page 9, enactments passed on the 2nd of July, the first conclusion concerns coordinating the wartime disposition of the military and police. The second conclusion, again going to pay, concerning the obligation to pay military and police members. And, sir, please pay particular attention to the fourth conclusion: "Prohibiting the individual release of persons from Trnopolje, Omarska, and Keraterm." And then flipping the page, page 10, to the enactments passed on the 24th of July, finally, the seventh decision, rationalising the public security service?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which one was that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 24th of July, page 10, decision number 7, rationalising the public security service, that being the local police. Sir, there is a lot of evidence from these conclusions, wouldn't you agree, that the Crisis Staff issued directions to the military and to the police and provided them with necessary support in concerning logistics and pay, for example?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: My comments are that it would appear as if there are several connections here. And yet, they are not fully explained in the rationale for why they were put in place, not fully explained. For example conclusion on page 9 that deals with prohibiting the release, the individual release of persons, from the three camps. What motivated that? What caused that? Was that to protect those persons if they were sent back out in the public domain? Would they be in more danger than if they were kept in the camp. So while I see these enactments, and while I understand the words that appear on the paper, I don't understand the rationale and the reason for many of them. While I can see the point that you've made about if your employee [sic] pays you, does he influence you, and you have presented me with documentation here that suggests that the civilian authorities at that level paid the military way, well, maybe that's the system that was in place. In maybe other armies that I'm familiar with, the funding for the military came from the top, from the federal government and down. Maybe in this system, the funding came from the top but it went through political channels down to the lowest level where the money was distributed. So I'm not so sure that it's important where the money was distributed from. The fact is that the civilian authorities somewhere along the line paid the bill and paid the wages of the people that were employed by the military. So I see a lot of declarations and enactments. Some of them I think one can take on face value and understand their reason and purpose, and some I don't understand and therefore can't really comment on -- from a professional standpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So your suggestion is that the conclusion prohibiting the individual release of persons from, for example, the Omarska camp, might have been taken to ensure the safety of those people, to keep them in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was only trying to point out that there must be a rationale for many of these decisions taken, and maybe that's rationale for that one and I selected that one because it seems to be a significant one and one that seems to be quite important. It stands out in stark relief. So if it stands out in stark relief, one must ask: Why did they do it that way? What happened? What caused this to take place? Why were these civilian authorities involved in this? So my point is I'm not sure that I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my suggestion to you is that in fact this conclusion shows that contrary to your opinion that the military was operating and maintaining the camps, that people were detained there on the decision of the Crisis Staff, they could not be released without the Crisis Staff approval, acting through Simo Drljaca, the chief of police and a member of the Crisis Staff. And let me put that to you. And before you answer, I would like to play a video. And it has not yet been marked. And I'd like the transcript -- it's very short, it's eight minutes long, Your Honour, to be distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Madam Registrar -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be marked S427, the video, and 427-1, the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The wrong video is on. There's another video that the Prosecution gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The video you intend to play is the except from video 000-2433. Correct? Interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: With Mr. Prcac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And Tariq Malik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be then be provisionally marked S427.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If we can hold it for a second, stop it for a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, just while it's being distributed, let me just explain, this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is an interview conducted by an investigator of the OTP, and this is Mr. Prcac, who was a member -- retired member of the Prijedor police who I believe has stated he was called back to duty to work at the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The transcript would be S427-1A.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If everyone has the transcript, we can proceed to play - I want to make sure the booths have the transcript, yes - to play the video. Excuse me, the booths are not ready yet, if we can wait a moment. I'm sorry. This is a nonsimultaneous translation, so that's why it takes eight minutes. Mr. Prcac will speak in Serbian, and then there's a translation into English. Just wait for a signal that the booths are ready. Okay. Okay, we can play the video, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: [Please refer to Exhibit S427-1A for videotranscript]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, just for your information, the people -- witnesses have said that approximately 120 names were called out from the Keraterm camp, but on buses that were then sent to Omarska.
