A group of bodies of over 120 bodies was exhumed in the municipality next to Prijedor, Sanski Most, and through DNA analysis, those that were identified were identified as being from among this group of 120 names called out at Keraterm and then sent to Omarska. Given what you've just heard, that Simo Drljaca signed this order, that 125 names from the Omarska camp were called out and then taken on these buses, isn't it abundantly clear that the authority to detain, to decide who would be in the camp and who would be taken out of the camp, that Simo Drljaca, a member of the Crisis Staff had that authority?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may have an objection, although I cautiously move on that in light of the Court's prior instruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, if my learned friend can point out where in the transcript it says that which he alleges and purports, if he can just show me on the two pages that we have where it mentions the Crisis Staff. I also have other objections in connection with this document, although the Court provisionally admitted it already. But we could address that outside the presence of the witness or perhaps at another time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think coming first to the last point, I think after one year of procedure, you should know it's not provisionally admitted, it is provisionally marked. This is an absolute different.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Second, related to the Crisis Staff, I think it wouldn't be too difficult to rephrase this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe I stated Simo Drljaca, a member of the Crisis Staff. I don't think that that's in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: To be very candid with the Court, it distorts obviously what this witness said, and he said that he was acting in a position that -- again, I don't want to argue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please don't argue. We are under the impression of that what we have heard, what we have seen in the transcript, and the witness is only asked to comment on this. And I think it's true, save you came to know the conclusions in the meantime, that Mr. Drljaca was, in fact, a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So please, let's hear the answer of the expert.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Drljaca is also a member of the police force, is he not?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Drljaca was the chief of the police for the Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: So in which role was he acting in this case when he went out with his bus and his vehicles and his guards and took these 120 people? Was he a police officer or was he a member of the Crisis Staff? It's not clear to me. I don't know which role he was playing, and so I really can't comment on the event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question was directed to your testimony regarding the military controlling and maintaining the camp. Is it clear that Simo Drljaca had the authority to take 125 people out of the camp, and does that affect your opinion that it was the military that ran the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said it was the military and the police in conjunction with each other. I think I said that I felt like the military was probably the ones that administered, operated, and maintained the camp, but I think I also said that the police were also involved. So if the chief of police of the area would show up at the camp, it might be very logical that those in charge of the camp at that moment, and I see it was a civilian gentleman who was a former police officer, retired, might very well turn over those 120 people. Maybe he simply knew no better. The fact of the matter is that here was a police chief, he was an authority. The police helped protect the camp, and he took away 120 people. I don't know if he was acting as a police officer or as a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, was the chief of police, Simo Drljaca, a professional policeman?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the word "professional" used in several documents. I presume that the word professional in those cases means that they are professionally trained and prepared to serve as police officers or military officers or whatever the profession might be. I'm not sure if the police chief was trained at some formalised institutions and worked his way through the ranks, patrolman and on up through the ranks of the police to become the chief or not. He may have been a political appointee. I'm not familiar with his background.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made the point I believe in your testimony that -- or perhaps it was in your report, that an officer, and in this case you were referring to the military, would be interested in pleasing his superiors, those who could appoint or promote him. Do you know how Simo Drljaca came to be the chief of police in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you mentioned that he could have been a political appointee. Would it matter, effect your view, as to how responsive he would to the political leadership if he was a political appointee appointed or elected at the municipal level as opposed to owing his position only to an appointment by the republic-level Minister of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: There could be -- there could be some differences here depending on the level from which he was appointed. But I would also assume that there must be some sort of a commissioning process or some sort of paperwork that the man would sign and agree to in which he pledges to do his very best and to be nonbiased and to not come under the influence of anyone, but to see his duty as he saw it. I'm only guessing there. But I would think that such documentation might exist and would put him on notice that he was to act as an individual and for the best good of the people that he was to please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if I told you that Simo Drljaca had the dubious background of being a lawyer by profession and had worked in the schools prior to being nominated for this position by a Serbian Municipal Assembly dominated by the SDS, would that affect your view of whether he would be responsive to the political leadership of the SDS in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think the part about him being an attorney would complicate the matter at all. That would mean to suggest to me that he was probably a very bright individual, number one. Not completely understanding the culture as it existed at that time and in that place, I'm not sure that I can comment on whether or not he would be responsive or who he would be responsive to. I simply can't give an answer. I don't know. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Part of your stove pipe analysis is that a subordinate reports to a superior regarding -- takes orders from, and then reports the results of those orders to the superior to which he is responsive. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe you said that the -- under the stove pipe, that person would not then be reporting to civilian leadership or responding to orders by the civilian authorities. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my experience, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown S114.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, giving you a little time to read this, this document is dated the 1st of July, 1992. The addressee, Crisis Staff of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. And that it indicates "In reference to your documents of the above numbers and dates, we hereby inform you that," and lists a series of conclusions, orders, and documents and decisions, and whether or not they are being complied with. Just to highlight a few, the first conclusion by which the release of prisoners is prohibited is being fully observed. Would that indicate to you that Mr. Drljaca was obeying the orders of the Crisis Staff regarding the release of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it indicates that that's taking place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown S - I believe it's 4-0 - S407.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, S407 is a document from the Ministry of the Interior Banja Luka, Security Services Centre, and indicates it's from the commission for the inspection of the municipalities Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, and Sanski Most police stations submitted a report concerning the situation as found and questions relating to prisoners, collection centres, resettlement, and the role of the SJB in connection with these activities. I just want to highlight a few sentences from this report in the interests of time. If we go to the first page, the second full paragraph in the fourth line, it indicates, "In order to solve the problem that had arisen, the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Prijedor decided to organise reception and accommodation in the settlement of Trnopolje for persons who sought protection, and that prisoners of war should be held for processing in the building of the Keraterm work organisation in Prijedor, or in the administrative building and workshop of the iron ore mine in Omarska." If we then turn the page and go to the fourth full paragraph, the first sentence, and it's referring above to the Keraterm facility, the fourth paragraph begins: "Pursuant to a decision of the Prijedor Municipality Crisis Staff, the army brought prisoners of war to this facility. The SJB was given the task of securing the facility with employees of the active and reserve forces of the police. The Banja Luka security services bureau and the Banja Luka corps command were informed about the capture of persons and were actively involved in the solution of the situation." And then on the same page, the last two lines indicate: "On 27 May, 1992, pursuant to the decision of the Crisis Staff of the Municipality of Prijedor, all the prisoners from the Keraterm facility in Prijedor were transferred to the facility in Omarska." Again, sir, is this report consistent with the view that Simo Drljaca and, in fact, the army, were bringing prisoners to these camps pursuant to a decision of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not clear to me. I think that the Crisis Staff of Prijedor established camps and said we can put them at this location, that location, and this location, and then the army and the police moved people to those facilities as space was available. I don't think this documentation shows that the Crisis Staff actually told them who to put where.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, General, this concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Very briefly, General, based on all that what you have read, seen, heard, is in your opinion any -- is there a slightest doubt that during the period of April through, say, September 1992, there was a state of armed conflict in the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: There certainly was, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I appreciate the clarity of your answers and the clear distinction between the setting up of a camp and running a camp. I think in part, you answered the question already. Who would be in charge to arrest persons that would be brought to these camps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, based on your question, I'm thinking about a combat situation. I'm thinking about an event where two forces meet somewhere, and someone raises their hands and drops their weapon. That is an arrest, I suppose, that word could be used, or someone is being captured. "Capture" is probably a better word for me. That person who is being captured would be moved off the front line immediately and interrogated to gather the immediate information they might have. And then all logic says that persons with others who have been captured should be moved to the rear to a camp where, first of all, they are taken from the battlefield and they are no longer a threat to the people that captured them. And number two, since they have been disarmed, they are now in a protected area. They are no longer in the combat. They are no longer in the combat situation. Then they are interrogated again. It's the military that makes arrest; it's the military that does that capturing in the scenario that I have painted for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then it would be consequent that the investigation could take place both by military and police within the camp. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: And by "investigation," sir, do you mean the interrogation of the captive? In my view, it would seem that the military would make further -- or conduct further interrogations, at least initially, to determine what else this individual may know about the battlefield and the deployment of enemy forces. I then see that it might be possible for that captive to be turned over to the police so that we could -- we could -- they could determine exactly who this person is. Are they really a combatant or are they a noncombatant who should end up ultimately being returned to their home? And so I can see maybe a two-tiered interrogation, unless it's very clear in the first case that the person who has been captured is a soldier, then I don't see the police interrogating them at all. If it's not clear, then I could see and understand why the police might want to know the equivalent of their security social number, their address, their place of work, and then sort out from all of that whether or not they are simply a noncombatant who was caught up in the combat situation and detained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If the result of this interrogation would be that a person allegedly has committed a crime, is under suspicion, what would be the next step?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, one would have to determine their status. Is that person who has been captured a military person of the opposing force? Is that person who has been captured simply a civilian? If that person is a civilian person, then it seems to me that they would eventually be turned over for investigation and the possible indictment to civilian authorities. If that person was military, then possibly the military would take some action to prosecute them based on the crimes that they had allegedly committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In front of which court?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say in the case of the military, it would be in front of a military court's martial. With regard to a civilian, I would presume it would be a civilian court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In case there is suspicion that the own military forces or members of these military forces allegedly have committed a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. crime, who would then be in charge of hearing these cases and preparing the indictment first?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's very clear. It would be the military force of which that person is a member. So if a soldier has committed a crime and he belongs to army A and he's investigated by army A, he's interrogated by army A, and he's brought to court martial by army A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Based on the documents and your entire research, you would know who would be the military court in charge for these crimes if so -- if committed in Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: My examination of the documents showed a clear representation of a military justice system within the army that evolved from the JNA. A court's martial system, a way of giving justice, offering justice, to a soldier who has committed a crime. So it's clear in those documents that such a system did exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So you would expect that in those cases you mentioned previously that would be under the jurisdiction of the military court, it has to be expected that the military court would act, and persons would be brought then to this military court. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. But then coming back to the two questions, setting up a camp and running a camp, the question of release was already discussed. But let's turn to another point. Would it be for the military to arrest an elected president of the Municipal Assembly of, say, Prijedor? Could there be any consolation that justifies the military to arrest the president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very interesting question with some very interesting implications. In my view, it's a situation where the military, if it had information that strongly suggested that the elected president is a criminal, then that information has to be turned over to the appropriate authority that has jurisdiction over that president. And I presume we're back to the police. I don't see that the military could arrest the civilian. It just doesn't seem to fit in my mind and in my experience. But if they had information that there was something wrong with this individual, then they have to turn it over to whoever has jurisdiction over them with regard to criminal actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the witness please be shown Exhibit Number S162-5B-1. Focus on the picture, yes. I take the liberty to read out that what we have received as the English translation of this article. "Subject: Arrest of Becir Medunjanin and his family. Yesterday, in one of the numerous dugouts in the village of Bezici of Kozarac, members of the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina captured Becir Medunjanin, another member of the Sana Una region war staff of Alija Izetbegovic's army. He was captured with his older son, Enes, and wife, Sadeta, and with Suad and Fehid Trnjanin, members of the Kozarac Crisis Staff. "The military carried out this operation of capturing Becir Medunjanin, the leader of the Muslim extremists of Kozarac, over a period of 15 days. Not a single soldier was wounded during the capture of Becir Medunjanin yesterday morning at about 8.00, while at the same time five members of the Green Berets were eliminated. They had been the personal security for the leader of the Kozarac Muslim extremists. "During the arrest, a considerable amount of documentation and arms were captured. Among them was a Winchester rifle, the personal weapon of Becir Medunjanin, who over the past few years had been proclaiming himself a great peacemaker." What would be your immediate comment on this text and the picture you can see?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, maybe I misunderstood your first question. I thought you were asking me would the military be authorised to arrest a civilian authority that is associated with that military organisation? But in this case, in the case that you've shown me here, it appears as if this gentleman was a leader of the extremist group --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's a totally different person.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Totally different situation. These two situations are not tied together. All right, fine. I would say that the military organisation that was in the area at the time found that this man was the leader of an extremist group, was therefore declared part of the threat and part of the enemy infrastructure. He was protected by five Green Berets, and so therefore, he was captured. And I don't know what his disposition was from there. But he was captured, and he was apparently taken away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And is there any justification to arrest at the same time the entire family and produce this humiliating situation as depicted here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely no justification for that. I'm sure the man's wife is not an enemy of the existing force or the public. And no, that's uncalled for, totally uncalled for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know what was the role of Becir Medunjanin before the takeover?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions. Judge --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, counsel asked me for the basis of my question about the 125 names called out. On the videotape we saw from the interview of Mr. Prcac. The testimony of Witness B regarding the names called out at the Keraterm camp is at page 2.243 of the trial transcript, and in the report of Mr. Sebire, he indicates that 126 bodies were exhumed in December 1998 at Hrastavo Glavica and discusses the identification of those bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Vassylenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: General, can you tell us what was the total numerical strength of Serbian military units in Prijedor Municipality before the Hambarine incident?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: What weapons were they armed with?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the documentation, it appears that they were armed with 105-millimetre Howitzers. They were armed with a certain number of tanks. I think they had a certain number of armoured personnel carriers. I didn't see any reference -- and obviously they had small arms for the infantrymen. I didn't see any reference to, for example, multiple rocket launchers or -- I didn't see any reference to - although they may have had available to them - anti-tank weapons. There's a possibility that they did have that sort of equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: My next question: What was total numerical strength of Bosnian Muslim armed units and how they were armed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen references to Muslim armed units up to 750 to 1250 people. It appears as if from the documentation that I saw that most of those people were armed with infantry weapons, sidearms. I think they did have some rocket launchers. In fact, I believe they destroyed a couple of tanks with rocket launchers. They certainly didn't as far as I can tell from the documentation I looked at, they didn't have any armoured vehicles. They didn't have any armoured personnel carriers. They didn't have any multiple rocket launchers. Obviously they didn't need any air defence equipment. So much of what you would see in the normal formation and layout of an army and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Much of what you would see in the normal layout of a table of organisation and equipment for a modern army was not available to them and they did not have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Then, General, was it feasible for the Muslims to provoke armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely feasible. If someone is shooting at you, even though it's coming out of a sidearm or a long gun, you might provoke Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. conflict that way. You might provoke combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: But was it feasible to provoke armed conflict hoping that they win this conflict?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about their expectations on winning. I can tell you that in Afghanistan, the Muslims there told me consistently that they would win and the Soviet army would be defeated. I couldn't understand it, I couldn't see it, but it worked. It happened. So I have no idea what their mental motivation may have been, their spiritual motivation. But somehow they were involved in this conflict, and I think people enter conflict with the idea they are going to be victorious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: In your report, page 40, you stated that the military response to the Hambarine incident lasted approximately six, seven hours. And -- but you didn't mention what was the area of the military operation? What was the battle zone? How large was the battle zone?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the documentation I looked at, it expanded from the point of the initial contact into a rather large area. I would presume that what happened was that the attacking force used reconnaissance by fire. They would go into an area, and they would begin firing. And if they received return fire, then they would continue into that area to clean up whatever resistance they came upon. And they probably used this tactic repeatedly, reconnaissance by fire, and they got fire in return. So that area expanded and expanded. I don't know ultimately how large it was. I'm not sure if we're talking about 100 square kilometres or 1.000 square kilometres. But I can see that that would be how this action would have unfolded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Was this area populated with civilians?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And that was one of the very significant problems, and sorting out and separating civilians and trying to keep from killing them and getting them involved must have been a very, very significant ordeal, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Have you any idea about the casualties among civilian population?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not, sir. But I imagine that there were -- there were many casualties. And it's an unfortunate, terribly unfortunate circumstance of warfare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: So can we come to the conclusion that armed forces were used indiscriminately and disproportionately in this situation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I'm going to come to that conclusion. I can simply tell you that there was one force that was disproportionately stronger and more well-equipped than the other. And so in the use of their weapons systems and their tactics, they may have made a disproportionate size attack and covered a disproportionate amount of territory. I don't know if they did it purposely, indiscriminately, or not. I simply know that it probably happened that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Yesterday, you stated that Serbian armed units overreacted.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Overreacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably did that in the context that there was an attack in that area called -- I believe it's Stari Grad. Excuse my pronunciation, and that they actually levelled that entire I will call it neighbourhood or suburb. I'm not familiar with the size nor the number of buildings there. But that is definitely, sir, an overreaction. And being a military person, it is disappointing to me to see when that sort of activity occurs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General, I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Argibay, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: No questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It is now for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Further examination by Mr. Ostojic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 31 of today's transcript, specifically line 1 through 3, General, you were asked by my learned friend at the OTP: "Anyone who is employed is influenced by those people who are paying their salaries." And your answer was in the affirmative, namely yes. Now, sir, would you think that if a military analyst such as you and Brown whose report you reviewed, would you think that his report, sir, since he's being employed and paid for by the OTP, do you think his report is influenced and the conclusions that he reviewed and the conclusions that he offered before this Court, do you think those would be influenced by the employer, namely the Prosecution, the very people who we are adversary to? Do you think that would influence him?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think as a concept, yes, he would be influenced. If I work for IBM, I'm going to be influenced by IBM. If they want me to wear a suit and tie every day, I wear a suit and tie every day. Why? Because in two weeks, they are going to give me my paycheque. Yes, the influence is there

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think, sir, as a military expert when you come into this Court and you don't review the military regulations of the very people or community in which you're going to offer testimony on, namely, the VRS or the JNA, do you think the Prosecution by omitting that and omitting and preventing Mr. Brown from reviewing those documents, do you think they may have influenced him so that he wouldn't render an opinion that would be considered objective, reasonable, and prudent before this Court?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that the wider body of knowledge that he reviewed looked at, took into consideration, would give him a broader base to respond to questions. If he was prevented or distracted from doing that by his employer, then it seems to me that that is somewhat of a failing and a shortcoming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other experts that testified by the OTP, if they were employed by the OTP, paid by the OTP, meaning the Office of the Prosecution, sorry, paid by the OTP, do you think that would influence their opinions as they gave? Let me just highlight some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just highlight some of them, Ms. Ewa Tabeau, a demographic, do you think her report would be influenced by her employer, namely the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think, sir, the police officer who may have testified in this case by the name of Mr. O'Donnell, do you think his testimony might be slightly influenced by the virtue of the fact that he receives a cheque by the very people who are adversary to us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think, sir, that this gentleman who did some, at least three exhumations, Nicolas Sebire, although he can't remember how many hours he spent working on a project, do you think he would be influenced by our adversaries over there because he receives a paycheque by them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think one of their criminal investigators, Mr. Inayat, do you think by him doing an analysis on documents for this Court, that he would do an objective report that would be neutral, or because he's getting paid by the OTP and is on regular salary by the OTP, do you think he would be influenced by the OTP as to what his conclusions might be, General?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, I don't pay you, but you are paid through the Tribunal. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we'll address --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I hope I'm paid a little bit by the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir I'd like to show you, if we may again, Exhibit 187, please. I think it was S187, and you were asked a couple questions in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. connection with page 6 of that document. Do you have that document on the ELMO, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apparently so. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it page 6 there? Now, the Office of the Prosecution asked you about a specific quote purportedly that Dr. Stakic made in this interview. And this interview apparently occurred, and I think we can stipulate to that, approximately six or so months after the events as they unfolded in the spring and summer of 1992. So I'm not sure of the exact month because it's not set forth in this document. But immediately above the section that the OTP referenced you, do you see, sir, at the top of the ELMO that Dr. Stakic says things such as "I am against war"? You're going too far now. It's right in the middle of the page there. Where it says: "No, I couldn't and not only because there were no signs of it, but because of my personal upbringing and stand." And then Dr. Stakic goes on to say: "I am against war." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet, I'm still looking for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Technician. They are zooming in to actually practically on the centre of the page.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it in the paragraph that starts with, "No, I couldn't."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, just continue to read that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Not only because there was no signs of it, but because of my personal upbringing and stand I am against war, against force. I am in the favour of reaching agreement."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you this, sir, about Dr. Stakic, although you came here as a military expert, if I gave you a hypothetical question that Dr. Stakic consistently before, during, and after the events of the spring and summer of 1994 [sic] continued to maintain a position of peace and continued to maintain a position of tranquility, would you describe Dr. Stakic as the OTP may have as Gandhi-like?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Objection, the hypothetical is not related to any facts in evidence. And as counsel pointed out, it's clearly beyond this witness's purported expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may reply, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't want to interfere, as I didn't with the Prosecution. But please remember that the Gandhi-like, this expression is already in evidence and apparently the Prosecution made reference to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand. If I may just respond quickly or reply to what my learned friend said, that there's no evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No argument, please in the moment. Put your question to the witness. The objection is dismissed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me move on to another point in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So does it mean that you don't want to have an answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: He can give us the answer. That would be fair.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you restate the question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure. If there was evidence in this case, and I strongly suggest, sir, there is, specifically if we look in November 1991, which is S-016-46A, if we look at the document that was marked and introduced into evidence of May 9th, 1992, so looking at the events, some evidence before the spring and summer of 1992, some during May 1992, some after, such as S187 that you just reviewed, and some even before that, but during the events, S261, and I'm citing that purely for my learned friend who had an objection that, and if Dr. Stakic consistently repeated the fact that he is in favour of peace and against war, and against using forces, how would you describe that, sir, as someone who would be inclined to influence the military to attack any enemy or would you describe that person as the OTP described others as Gandhi-like?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, the last part of the question is not correct. It was not the OTP describing Dr. -- another person as Gandhi-like.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would describe that person as reasonable. I would describe that person as a person who confined -- who can find alternatives to problems. I would describe that person as a person who is diplomatic. I would describe that person as one who is searching for solutions that don't require man's -- in humanity demand to be exercised. I was a soldier. I guess it's still in my blood. But if there's never another war, then I would be very, very happy indeed. We do not need war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We couldn't agree with you more, General. Let me ask you this, sir: With respect to the attack on Kozarac, May 24th, 1992, you were asked with respect to the arming of the Muslims at the checkpoint, and I think they described a Winchester rifle that may have been used, as your report indicates, sir, and as is quite clear, two tanks were destroyed during that attack. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you, sir, under any consideration would opine that those two tanks that the military, namely the VRS, had while they were proceeding on the Prijedor/Banja Luka Road on or about May 24th, 1992, do you think those Winchester rifles had the capacity or the capability to destroy either one of those tanks?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So those persons that were at this checkpoint who initially provoked and killed one of the military personnel, were they armed more significantly than just with hand-held guns and Winchester rifles?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why is it so obvious?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because you don't destroy two tanks with a sidearm or a long gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, we talked about some influence that Dr. Stakic purportedly had between the police and the military. I perhaps was neglectful in not showing you documents, but presume this as being true. Unless of course there is an objection. If Dr. Stakic had a brother-in-law who was mobilised in the military and there was a request by the brother-in-law's family to release him from the military, and Dr. Stakic could not and did not release that individual, namely his brother-in-law from the military, and that young man ultimately died as a result of his service, would that indicate to you that Dr. Stakic had any influence over the military if he couldn't get his own brother-in-law out of the military?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't sound like he had any influence, because if he did, he would certainly have been get his brother-in-law out from under that military obligation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Same question, sir: What if Dr. Stakic hypothetically had a young nephew from his wife that also was mobilised and also died as a result of the events in the spring and summer of 1992 and also was asked to see if he could influence anyone to release that individual from the military, and yet Dr. Stakic couldn't and didn't, and that young nephew of his ultimately perished. Would that, sir, indicate that Dr. Stakic had influence over the military?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't suggest that he had influence over the military. No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doesn't it, in fact, sir, suggest quite the opposite, that he had no influence whatsoever, and Dr. Stakic couldn't, despite the fact that he was president of a municipality, he couldn't have any power and didn't have any power whatsoever even to have one of his relatives released or relieved from military duties during the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it looks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's talk a little bit about reasonableness and being prudent as a military person. Sir, if a military is taking a convoy through a road, is it required, sir, to take side roads to avoid potential conflict, or does it, sir, in a reasonable and prudent manner advise the potential individuals who would be considered the enemy, for example, on May 24th, 1992, it's prudent is it not, and reasonable, is it not, that the military would issue an ultimatum advising those persons at the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. checkpoint that they are passing through, informing them that they are passing through and only seek safe passage? Is that reasonable that that's what the military should do?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that that's more than reasonable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Likewise, turning to the events of May 22nd, the attack on Hambarine, was it reasonable for the military and was it prudent for the military prior to immediately engaging the individuals at the checkpoint to first request that the perpetrators of the crime, namely the killing of two VRS soldiers and the wounding of two others, that they issue a request that the perpetrators of that crime be turned over? Is that reasonable and prudent?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's very reasonable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what they did in this case. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the perpetrators of those crimes did not and refused to otherwise surrender the individuals at issue, and the military subsequent to that issued another ultimatum that advised them that if the perpetrators were not turned over, they were going to go into the hamlet, find them, and then attack ensued. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you this about the political people in the community --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and witness make a break between question and answer, please, and can the counsel slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for being patient thus far. I will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you think it's irresponsible of the civilian authorities once they learn of the fact that members of the military were shot, killed, injured, is it irresponsible for them to issue a public announcement telling the people of the village of Hambarine that there is an event that may occur, that the military has informed everyone of, that the military has obviously issued an ultimatum warning the civilians about the situation so that there can be safety? Is that reasonable for the civilians to do so or unreasonable?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's very reasonable. It's a cooperative effort. They are cooperating with the military, and they are helping to notify the population so that in the end, there will be a good result possibly and a result that doesn't require combat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we only have about 15 more minutes, and I don't know that it's necessary to break, but I'll obviously defer to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think so, because we have to discuss the admission of evidence in the presence of the expert. Maybe he can assist us in this exercise. And therefore, without any doubt, we have to continue as envisaged at quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, Your Honour. Just wanted clarification. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, with the Court's permission and the assistance of the usher, can you be shown Exhibit S426. Sir, you're looking at what was previously identified or is identified as S426. There were some questions from counsel regarding that document dated the 3rd of August, 1992. Sir, isn't it correct that that document does not show on the distribution list the civilians or Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this document, sir, clearly shows, or at least you could help me with this, that there was a verbal order from the army main staff permitting a visit by the international committee and a team of reporters to the detention camps, Manjaca, Trnopolje, Omarska, and they identify Prijedor within the next two. Sir, doesn't this order indicate and in fact it wasn't the civilian authorities who approved or allowed the visit to these detention centres or camps, but in fact it was the army main staff commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army main staff commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the fourth paragraph on that, it also identifies that the chief of security shall appoint a security officer from the 1st Krajina Corps to escort the international committee.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who's issuing this order to the chief of security, the military or the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military. It's for the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during the times of threat of war, imminent threat of war, or a state of war, when there's a mobilisation that's on the territory, the military can mobilise as you've stated in your report and from the documents that you've reviewed, the military can mobilise property as well as individuals including police reservists and active policemen. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you, sir, a Defence 65 ter number 356, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You may, but please be aware that we didn't decide on the amendment of the exhibit list in this part. We are still with Document 249. Then there is a gap. And then it restarts with 560.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It should be in one of his binders.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What are we looking for?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There are some markings on this, but we could place this on the ELMO. That would be fine. 356.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, just so we could speed this up in the couple minutes that we have, this is a document from the 1st Krajina Corps command dated the 9th of June, 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Below, if we can just have the technician assist us, or the usher, so that we may look at the highlighted portion.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 4 in this case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're talking on this date, early on to the events of the spring and summer 1992, namely, the 9th of June, 1992. Correct? And does it not show here that the military is identifying problems related to the functioning of the civil authorities. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, in your review of the documents within those seven or so binders that are before you, did you see a consistent pattern where the military were complaining about the inefficiency and the lack of functionality of the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What binder is that in, if you can point out those documents for us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in volume 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, there are many, if not an exhaustive amount of documents, which show among other things that civilian authorities according to the military had lost their functionality and in fact have been inefficient during the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would you find it somewhat surprising that the OTP military expert, when he testified in this case, didn't look at those very documents, and for some reason during his testimony, he didn't review those documents but claims to the Court that he's giving an objective opinion in connection with the relationship between the civilians and the military, and the civilians and the police? Don't you, sir, think that as a reasonable person in order to claim that you're giving an objective opinion, you should review the documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, I can't admit such a hypothetical and, to a certain extent, even unfair question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If Your Honour will remember, there were 90 documents that were given to us pursuant to Rule 68 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We should not discuss this in the presence of an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me show you the next document which is 65 ter number 368, with the assistance of the usher. This is a document, sir, dated the 17th of June, 1992, and I'll direct your attention first to the first page so that you can tell us who created the document or from what source it comes from.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It came from the corps command in this case, 1st Krajina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention, sir, to the second page of that document. And during that date that we've just identified based upon that document, which was the 17th of June, 1992, does the military, sir, report their awareness of activity by smaller extremist SDS, Serbian democratic party, groups clashing with our units since looting is their motive for fighting?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the VRS, which is the military, 1st Krajina, both 5th Kozara as well as the 43rd Motorised Brigade, composed according to the OTP of solely Serbian soldiers ethnically pronounced, here in their report as early as June 17th, 1992, the military itself is using a word which I'm going to have you define as "clashing" with SDS, namely Serbian, extremist as the word is reflected. First define for me what that word militarily speaking "clashing" means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means they're fighting. They are meeting each other in firefights probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that significant, sir, for the military since members of the SDS, which is the party that purportedly was in control of the Prijedor Municipality, that the military in light of this would be less reluctant to take orders from any civilians, not to take instruction from any civilians, because, in fact, as early as the 17th of June, 1992, they were, in fact, clashing with the very members that the OTP claims that they are taking instruction and direction from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's time now for the break. But before, we should provisionally mark those documents provisionally marked as 65 ter 356, Defence. This would be D110. And the provisional 65 ter 368 of the Defence would be D111. The trial stays adjourned until quarter past 2.00, continued in Courtroom I. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.37 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Please be seated. May we add to the appearances that the Prosecution is now represented also by Ms. Joanna Korner. And without further ado, please continue, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General Wilmot.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, just going to just try to walk you through --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's microphones are not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you can just click the little buttons for your microphone, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, after the three attacks or incidents that we were discussing today, namely Hambarine, Kozarac, and the city/town of Prijedor, I want to show you a couple of exhibits that followed those events from our 65 ter list number. With the Court's permission and the usher's assistance, we would like to show you 65 ter number 357 document dated the 8th of June from the 1st Krajina Corps and have that placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm getting Serbian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would then be provisionally marked D111. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 112, then, okay. We have to come to the question of whether it's already 65 terred or not. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Wilmot, are you able to hear me in English?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had possibly Serbian in the background. I was trying to eliminate that. I think it's done now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, looking at this exhibit that's in front of you dated the 8th of June, 1992, there's some highlighted marks there. And it's a military report, obviously, issued to the main staff, which is their daily report, and it cites there where it's highlighted, even though it's approximately nine days since the attack on the city/town of Prijedor, "there continues to be some activity and there continues to be a conflict still in the area," does it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Specifically in the area of the Prijedor/Banja Luka Road where the incident on May 24th, 1992, occurred when the convoy attempted to pass and it was provoked and ultimately resulted in retaliation or a response by the military.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, if the technician can scan just a little further out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we're looking at paragraph 8 or I'm directing your attention to paragraph 8, there seems to be a comment issued by the military that's highlighted there. Can you tell me what that says.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Energetic measures are still being taken to prevent crime and the war profiteering."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that mean, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It sounds as if there are rogue bands and thugs travelling throughout the area, and there is energetic response to take them under task and prevent them from profiteering in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me take you to another document, if I may, and have the Madam Registrar give you Document Exhibit S407, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be provisionally D113.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, it's already Exhibit S407, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think we're referring to the prior document, are we not, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's extremely difficult --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- The exercise you are doing today is -- I have to be careful with my words, but receiving a stack of documents in a case this morning, and then expecting that we are ready to discuss these documents immediately, this is not the way a court should proceed. But we have to take into account the interest of the expert, being here only today. And therefore as an exception, unfortunately we have to proceed this way. But don't be surprised that a lot of confusion will emanate from this, and I have to emphasise that there was no one decision amending the exhibit lists of the Defence related to these documents you're providing us now. Only that the transcript is clear on this. So Madam Registrar, please once again, the document we have before us now is?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: S407, Your Honour. And if I'm correct, we only used one 65 ter document, 357, which is marked D112. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, just can you help me with what's the date of the document, Exhibit S407, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: 14 August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The military in our report in our 65 ter number of a document that was provided to us by the OTP dated the 22nd of August, 1992, Exhibit 411, Defence 65 ter, it states in that report "the report states that after foreign reporters visited Omarska and Trnopolje, nobody wants to accept the responsibility for orders for mass deportation of civilians in the camps." And that's 411. When you look at S407, and the Prosecutor asked you questions about the establishment of the camp, can you please turn to page 4 of that document. And tell me how many people does Mr. Simo Drljaca report that have been killed or died at the detention centres? It's in the first paragraph, I believe the first two lines.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says two persons of Muslim ethnicity died of natural causes, and 49 persons left the investigation centre in an unknown manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I don't want you to speculate, but would it be a reasonable assumption to conclude that Mr. Simo Drljaca was, in fact, reporting things that were inaccurate and untrue?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could very well be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on the evidence, sir, that you reviewed, and I believe that there's no dispute, from the outset of the case there was no dispute, as to the number of Muslims citizens who lost their lives regrettably in those detention centres, do you think that Mr. Simo Drljaca was accurate when he said that two had lost their lives, or was he simply as the report on 65 ter number 411, simply trying to cover up or blame others?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could very well be that he was understating the facts to cover up some situation that he didn't want to have revealed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that same report, S407, where Mr. Drljaca states that the camps were established purportedly by the Crisis Staff, can we take that at face value given the fact that he completely distorts the number of the victims that suffered during the spring and summer of 1992 in those detention centres?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could very well be an inaccuracy also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may show you just one or two more exhibits, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: D12 to be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this is an exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may just proceed while we're getting the document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is an exhibit that you listed on your report as you had reviewed, I'd like you to turn to the second page of that exhibit, though it seems to be -- page 2 on the bottom, sir. And does it say on the top the ERN number L, as in Larry, 0001605?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's a translator's note on that exhibit, sir, and within that exhibit, it states on the third sentence, which starts on the third line proceeding on the fourth line: "The statement seems unbiased, and is equally critical of Muslims and Serbs." It continues. This statement that a Muslim individual who was apparently within the Green Berets or the Patriotic League or some other paramilitary formation in the Prijedor Municipality certainly seems to be from your review as well, sir, unbiased. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you relied on that report. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it surprise you, sir, that if an expert offered by the OTP, a military analyst, was giving testimony and what he claimed to be objective but he did not review such a report from a Muslim who gave a rather exhaustive detailed recount of the activities as they existed in the spring and summer of 1992 in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Does counsel have a page to cite. I don't believe that was Mr. Brown's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's my very point. He did not review that document at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: My recollection is that Mr. Brown said that he did review that document, and it's cited in his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: My apologies. I'll refer to the page. If that's true, I'll withdraw the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And at the same time, I would ask you kindly to refrain from unnecessary comments such "he claimed to be objective." I think we should take it that in principle, everybody works as objective as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you this document, if I may, sir, that was given to us by the OTP which has the ERN number I believe it's 004, looks like 81850, if we could place that on the ELMO with the Court's permission, of course. Sir, this is a document dated the 19th of July, 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There seems to be on the very first sentence of this document an issue that is attempted to be resolved regarding the superiority or the chain of command, as placed in the parenthesis, between the MUP, which we've established is the Ministry of the Interior, which is the police, and the army. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just so we can follow, is there an exhibit number or a 65 ter number or do you have a copy that we could follow along with?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's my only copy, and I've misplaced the 65 ter number, but it's clearly a document that was offered by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think we can't really proceed this way. You come out of the blue with documents without any numbers, without reference. So please, do the necessary, drop the question now. You may ask for copies, but we are not prepared to work without copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, Your Honour. We'll withdraw the question at this time, and we have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If the witness could just be shown D111. It was shown at the end of this morning. Further cross-examination by Mr. Koumjian:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can put my copy on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 356.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You're welcome to use my copy and just put it on the ELMO. First page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to remind us all, this was the document that referred to SDS paramilitaries clashing with the 1 KKR troops. Sir, this is a report of the 1st Krajina Corps of the situation in the territory of the corps. Can you read the names of the municipalities in the section -- or perhaps I could read them, given I have a little more familiarity, a bit more, with the pronunciation probably. Bjelovar, Virovitica, Podravska Slatina, Bosanska Dubica, Nova Gradska, Slovanska Pozega, Prijedor, Banja Luka, Derventa, Lamac, Jajce, and Zenica. Sir, do you know how far these municipalities such as Jajce and Zenica are from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if the SDS paramilitaries referred to in that report were in Prijedor or in one of the other municipalities named?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can move on. I'm done with that document. Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown S187.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that document this morning, Mr. Ostojic asked you about a statement by Dr. Stakic "I am against war." Sir, in your experience, have you heard politicians giving public statements, politicians, leaders, dictators, any of these individuals giving public statements saying that they are in favour of war, or is it more common for them to portray themselves publicly as peacemakers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if you could take 10.000 politicians and take 10.000 statements and take some kind of an average how it would come out. But it seems to me that most of the politicians would say to the public, We are for peaceful solutions to problems. That's probably how it would come out. But I don't have any statistical knowledge of that. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you think of any political leader, dictator, who stated: "I'm in favour of war" or "I'm not in favour of peace"? Can you think of a single instance where a person made that statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depends on the environment and the circumstances, I suppose. In very recent times, our own president, Mr. Bush, seems to be in favour of military action because of the circumstance that he thinks he finds himself in. He thinks he's -- he thinks that his nation is threatened by weapons of mass destruction, and so he has offered several statements and speeches that would suggest that he wanted to get the international community to back him and go to war, and it looks like that's what's happened. So it depends, very much, sir, on the environment and on the conditions that exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And trying to avoid any recent controversial events, would it be correct to say then that even someone in favour in war is likely to portray themselves as responding to some threat that they envision?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We object to the form of the question. It calls for speculation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sustained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, we talked about the difference between civilian and military. Is there some common way of recognising who was a civilian and who was a military official?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite often it's a uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Civilians do not wear uniforms. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, they do not, although there are some uniforms that they wear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Boy scouts.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: A bit outrageous, I suppose, like doormen and people that belong to the salvation army and so forth. So some of them wear uniforms, but normally we can identify military people by uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You were asked this morning about mobilisation and the ability of a person with influence in the military to exempt their friends or relatives from mobilisation. Sir, you achieved a very high rank in the military. And you commanded a large force, correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you clearly were within the military chain of command. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, first of all, did you have the authority to exempt, if there had been a draft in the United States, to exempt your friends from that draft?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the situation that I was in and in the institution that I was in and in the rules that apply to it, no way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, would a person -- is it generally seen as a patriotic duty and a legal duty to respond to a mobilisation and not to use individual connections to exempt your friends and relatives?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is seen generally as a patriotic duty and a legal duty to respond to mobilisation. But then there are ways to respond at different levels and different echelons and different commitments. For example, there are reserve forces, there are national guard forces. And we have sometimes found where people of influence direct their youngsters or their nephews or whoever the case may be into a national guard situation as opposed to a regular army situation to avoid possible exposure to combat. So while in general it's patriotic and so forth, there are ways to even in the institution that I am talking about today, there are ways to avert, to avoid exposure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is it actually your opinion that you can draw an inference from the fact that Dr. Stakic's brother-in-law was mobilised, you can draw an inference that he did not have influence over the 43rd Brigade in Prijedor because of that fact?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very difficult question, and I don't think it's one that I can answer, not being fully aware of the culture and the relationship here and the situation and the environment that existed. I don't know. If someone, not Dr. Stakic in this case, but, for example, someone with a great amount of money could get arranged and buy somebody out of the military, there are all sorts of ways of doing this, and I'm not sure what might have existed here and how this system exactly worked. But there's a possibility that Dr. Stakic, if he was very well-connected could get a relation out of being involved in the military. And then on the other hand, there's the possibility that he couldn't do it at all no matter how connected he was. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you were a politician who sought -- wanted to keep your public image clean and, two, you supported a war that you thought was patriotic, wouldn't you not attempt to influence a mobilisation decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Object to the form of the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's a fair question to a military expert.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably would avoid trying to influence a decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were shown a document this morning about the visit of foreign journalists to Manjaca and to the Omarska camp, and order from General Talic to his command. I want to direct you to something you may or may not have read, and that is the testimony of Mr. Edward Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We could hand out the copies of the transcript so that the Court and counsel can follow. We have some more copies. Hopefully everyone has page 7.922 of the trial transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in this particular moment of the trial, a journalist from -- who was on that visit to the camps that I believe you indicated you had seen some of that video, Mr. Edward Vulliamy was testifying about a meeting at the Municipal Assembly building with several individuals, including Colonel Arsic and Dr. Stakic. And beginning on line 24, you see that there was a question to Mr. Vulliamy, "You indicated and perhaps I missed something, you indicated that Colonel Arsic encouraged you to go to Manjaca. How was it that that was finally resolved?" And the answer from Mr. Vulliamy was: "I mean, it wasn't resolved. It was resolved by us refusing to go to Manjaca and saying that that's not where we were going to go. Then he said, "If you want to go to Omarska, these are the people you need to talk to.'" Question: "You just made a gesture to your right. Was that what Colonel Arsic did? Is that a gesture he made or explain what you meant. Mr. Vulliamy said: "He made a gesture. I don't know whether he said it by name. And he gestured towards Mr. Kovacevic and Mr. Stakic." For your information, Mr. Kovacevic was a civilian official in the Crisis Staff. Finally, sir, before you answer this question, I'd like to refer you to one short section of S187, page 2. I know the tape was there, I don't know if the tape was cued this morning. So I'm just going to read the particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it might be helpful. Is it prepared already?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I did not cue the tape. The tape is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No tape. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 2, and we can hand that out also. It's a very short section of the interview with Dr. Stakic. We have at least three copies, four, five. Sir, in the section marked, the reporter asked Dr. Stakic: "There have been reports in the British press about centres of Omarska and Trnopolje and places like that. Do the authorities in Prijedor have any control or have they had control over places like that?" Dr. Stakic answered: "These places, such as Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje were a necessity in a given moment, and were formed according to a decision of the civilian authorities in Prijedor."
