Reporter: "So these three camps or how are they" -- Dr. Stakic: "Reception centres." Reporter: "Reception centres were formed according to the decision of your civilian authorities?" Dr. Stakic: "Yes, yes. As I have said, this was a necessity in a given moment when there was no longer any possibility to resolve the question of relations and division of power through agreement by peaceful means, and when extremists from the ranks of the SDA and the HDZ party, but mostly the SDA, which won here and which at one point lost control and started using force, murdering members of the army and the police. We had to set up such centres." Sir, given the fact that Colonel Arsic indicated that the reporters needed the authority of the civilians, Kovacevic and Stakic, to visit Omarska, given what you just heard Dr. Stakic say about what he called "reception centres" having been formed by the civilian authorities, and that "we had to set up such centres," is it still your opinion that Dr. Stakic did not have influence and control of the Omarska and Keraterm camps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the second document that you've given to me, Dr. Stakic is interfacing with a reporter. And he doesn't exactly explain why camps had to be set up. He didn't go on to say that we had to set up the camps because people were being detained and people were being questioned and people were being brought in to a central location. He didn't say that. He didn't say "that's why we set up the camps." And so I don't think that this exchange with the press, with this reporter goes far enough to explain the why the camps were set up. And I go back again to my original idea that the civilians did set up the camps, the civilians did choose the site for the camps because they are the ones that are on the ground and know what facilities might be available. In the case of the other exchange, is the implication here that they had to go to one camp and not the other? We're talking about body language and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me make this clear, sir.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The evidence is that the Manjaca camp was a strictly military camp run by the military; that the Omarska camp had a commander that was police, Defence witnesses who worked at that camp said that the police provided the security and the army provided an outer ring, perimeter security. So, sir, that's in answer to your question about the difference with the Manjaca and Omarska camp. Given that background, do you see that it's quite obvious that it was the Crisis Staff, Dr. Stakic and Kovacevic, that had the authority to allow the visit to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they could provide -- I think they could make a decision to allow the visit to one particular camp as opposed to another, but I don't see how that ties into operating and maintaining and administering the camp. And so I think it was just something that these people agreed to. You go to that camp and not this one. I don't see that it's a smoking gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Wilmot, do you believe that you have provided this Chamber with an objective view of the events and the crimes that occurred in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hopefully, I have. Yes, I do believe that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you referred this morning to Becir Medunjanin as an extremist. Why did you choose that word, to describe Becir Medunjanin as an extremist?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the form of the question. I'd like to be heard on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I hear the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think when the Court asked the question, the article was placed in front of General Wilmot. It was clear that he read from the article and did not formulate an opinion, and questions prior to that clearly stated and suggested he didn't know what capacity he held, he didn't know what his function was at that point. I think that it's unfair to distort the record to claim that General Wilmot called Becir Medunjanin an extremist or anyone else for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think this is a fair statement, and it's -- that's indeed what you did. You read out the article.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Following Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I think the word "extremist" was in the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This was in the article, and then later on, I did not continue because you stated that you wouldn't know Mr. Medunjanin. So therefore... But it's for the Prosecution to proceed in this line of questions related to Mr. Medunjanin. And what about --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I presume you adopt Mr. Ostojic's position about why you used that word.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will object to form of the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, the expert did not use himself and attributed the word "extremist" to Mr. Medunjanin. The question is only that apparently the expert doesn't know who was Mr. Medunjanin. If you want to proceed, then it's for the Prosecution to go ahead and tell about who this person was in the past, and about the fate of this person. I think this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just to conclude --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to be clear, and I'm almost, the answer on page 57 of today's LiveNote, when Your Honour was questioning him about the capture of Mr. Medunjanin, at line 14, the witness said: "I would say that the military organisation that was in the area of the time found that this man was the leader of the extremist group, was therefore declared part of the threat, part of the enemy infrastructure." So I stand corrected, and at least in what I've just read, you called him the leader of the extremist group. General, why did you call him the leader of the extremist group? Why did you call the group of people defending Kozarac extremists?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because you've handed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, same basis.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- You've handed me dozens of pages of documents, and the word "extremist" was on the document, and I picked up on it and I looked at the picture and I saw that the man was being captured, that he was being taken into custody, and unfortunately his family was with him. And I used the word "extremist" because it was on the piece of paper. I don't know if he is an extremist not, but it was on the paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, in all of the references that you used, those were statements by Dr. Stakic, by the SDS, or by the VRS army. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean that they were the authors and the instigators who used the word "extremist"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure I know who identified and said and pointed at this man and said "you're an extremist" and had it published in a newspaper. But if you say that's where it came from, then the possibility certainly exists. I only used the word because it was on the piece of paper that was presented to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe it can exist, in fact, the expert if Prosecution gives a little bit of the background of Mr. Medunjanin and the fate of Mr. Medunjanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the evidence that has been presented that is unrefuted is that Mr. Medunjanin held the position, a civilian position, of secretary of the secretariat for national defence in Prijedor in the elected multiethnic assembly. There also is evidence that Mr. Medunjanin participated in the defence of Kozarac. He has been identified in some documents as the leader of the defence of Kozarac. And the evidence was that he was placed in the Omarska camp, beaten to death, and died in the camp. Do any of those facts make you conclude that he was an extremist? And let me add, his wife was taken from the camp on the bus, and her body has been exhumed.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none of those facts make me believe he was an extremist, and I say again for clarification I only used the word because I saw it on the piece of paper, the document that was handed to me. I'm very sorry that this happened to this gentleman and to his wife, and it's a terrible circumstance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you see any justification for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I noticed on your resume that you listed yourself as a consultant for McBreen and Kopko. I may be mispronouncing that. Can you explain that work.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's on my resume because I see myself these days as having two jobs, being a private consultant, and also being an employee of the Steele Foundation. And so any time I pick up a new consultancy, I simply add it to my resume so that it looks more rounded and full. I was called by McBreen and Kopko and asked if I could be an expert witness, and when that happened, when I accepted the job, I put it on my resume.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that refers to your work in this case. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you testified on page 14.067 of yesterday's transcript, I asked you about having read Mr. Brown's report, Ewan Brown, and I said, "Can you tell us if you say any factual errors in Mr. Brown's report." And you said: "No, I don't think I saw any factual errors. In his cross-examination, I see where he and I agree on many points concerning the events that took place at the time, so there was compatibility and essentially I think we agreed on the doctrine." Do you want to correct that or stand by that answer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the doctrine where we generally agreed, and that's where I would come down the strongest. He talked about the words "coordination" and "cooperation," and there are many things that he said that I agree with in terms of doctrine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, given your review of Mr. Brown's report, and your review and use of Mr. Butler's report, would it be correct to say that you find the work of these military analysts for the Office of the Prosecutor reliable, reliable enough to use them in your own report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, what they said is very reliable. What they said is quite proper in several instances. I suppose there are differences in when we take a look at did they go far enough, did they look at the other side of the coin, and did they consider the larger picture? So that's probably where some of the differences appear and occur in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Defence? Further examination by Mr. Ostojic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, just a couple questions if I may, on page 12 of today's transcript, Mr. Koumjian from the Office of the Prosecution asked you if a politician wanted to exempt an individual and wanted to keep his public image and continue to support a war effort. Sir, would this politician, if he had a brother-in-law and/or a nephew, would he at the very at least, if he had any influence over the military as alleged, would he use any influence that he had to move these individual, or these individuals, his brother-in-law and his nephew, from the front lines where they would, as in this case, indeed perish? Wouldn't you expect that to be a reasonable, a logical, and a prudent thing for a politician to do? In order that his relatives don't see battle, he would move them in area, perhaps a desk job, or in some other facility as opposed to allowing them to continue to be in the front?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that as -- is this working? I see that as an option that a politician of influence could certainly take. Maybe recognising that he can't prevent his relative from being mobilised, from being drafted into the military, okay, allow that to happen, and then once he's in see if he can influence the position he takes up and keep him out of harm's way if possible. So yes, that could very well happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Koumjian from the Office of the Prosecution also asked you on page 10, "Did you have the authority to exempt your friends from the draft?" And your answer was essentially "no way." Sir, my question to you is: If you wanted to, could you have any your influence with your connections being a brigadier general at the time to move people from either the front line, to move them to a desk job if you so desired? Could you use any influence or did you have any influence to do so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, at the time I was in the military, I didn't have any relatives in the military. But I can tell you this: There were certain people in the military who were especially talented and that I caused them to change positions and locations because I wanted them to work for me. So I did have that kind of influence. I wanted Sergeant A to come and work for me in the Pentagon. Now, Sergeant A may have been in Vietnam, in combat, in a combat situation. And because I needed him and because he could help me with pressing business, I could very well influence his assignment and get him assigned to the Pentagon. So yes, that's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think, sir, from common knowledge that we see in the papers that we can perhaps take judicial notice of that when former presidents or former presidents of countries have their sons and daughters in a time of war not serve on the direct front line but they are actually removed to reserve forces or to areas of safety? Did that ever occur based upon your experience or knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, the current president of the United States, sir, one of the main problems and criticisms of him is that his father was the former director of CIA, former vice-president, and then former president of the United States exercised his influence at the time in order to avoid that his son and his children, including the governor of the state of Florida, to avoid military service at the time when there was a callup. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time, the first Mr. George Bush was the director at some time for the CIA, and he exercised that influence. Dr. Stakic, is there any evidence that you saw, sir, from the documents that he had the power or the ability to influence any of the military in any way whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I have one question of Mr. Ostojic's that I don't believe the General answered. Further cross-examination by Mr. Koumjian:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, would you take your friends off the front line because they were your friends? Would that be ethnical?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said. I said if there was an extremely talented person --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you to answer my question. That's not my question. My question was would you take your friends off the front line because they were your friends?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Defence, any other questions? I can't see any. I can't, unfortunately, yet excuse you because beforehand, we have to go into some details of the exhibits tendered during your testimony. Let me start with, I hope, the easiest exercise. This would be the video. This was tendered today by the Prosecution as S427. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Court can just refresh my recollection, is that the eight-minute video and the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Interview of Dragoljub Prcac by Tariq, Malik.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes we do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For what reasons, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We think that the evidence should be excluded for a number of reasons, Your Honour. We believe that proceeding in the manner and producing evidence at this late stage is clearly an attempt to surprise the defendants with facts that have not been but were clearly in the possession of the Office of the Prosecution from the beginning of this case. If their position was X, they should have produced the documents. To present this evidence now is highly prejudicial. The Defence also believes and objects to the fact that we did not have an opportunity, which is protected under a fundamental right of these rules in this Tribunal, to cross-examine this individual. Instead, we get a statement from this individual in part, although this individual may have given other statements from my understanding he has, the complete record of his statement is not before the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure if the Defence position is that any evidence that was produced in the last day or two does not come into evidence, because they have produced an awful lot of evidence in the last day or two. This was in response specifically, it's proper rebuttal, in response to the testimony of their expert which was very strong that only the military controlled the camps and the detainees. This directly contradicted that. As to the right to cross-examine this witness, first, the Tribunal rules do allow hearsay, as counsel knows. Furthermore, unfortunately, this witness is not available. He has an appeal pending before the Tribunal. So he's not available as a witness, and for that reason, we believe it's proper and relevant evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: After deliberations, admitted into evidence as S427. Then we had S426. Madam Registrar, if you could assist me, please, this was, if I'm correct, the document from 3 August 1992, 1st Krajina Corps command. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence S426A and B respectively. Then let's turn to the tendered documents by the Defence. The first question goes to the Prosecution under the headline right to be heard. We are confronted with a motion of 3rd March where the Defence requests leave to submit Exhibits 561 to 566, and then in addition, we were provided only today with exhibits 250 through 560. I think I had no chance to have a look on these documents. Are there any principle objections against this procedure?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say, we're all rather confused at the moment as to where we are on the Defence exhibits, and that's why I came in because we divided the exhibits between us. We were given a list, proposed exhibit list, which runs from 1 to 560. Then when the expert Dr. Trifkovic came, three volumes of documents were produced which ran from numbers 1 up until I think 500. And then we were given some further additional exhibits last night. Your Honour, between the three of us, we have gone through the exhibits that were on the original list, and by and large, we agree that most of them are admissible, and each of us has marked the ones we would consider inadmissible for the reasons, and that's a small bunch, either relevance or other matters. So, Your Honour, are you now talking about the whole set of exhibits or?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we have to follow the rules and therefore go set by step.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The first step would be, no doubt, to decide on the Defence request to amend the exhibit list. This was a motion dated March 3, 2003, related to Exhibit Numbers 561 through 566. Any objections against --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There's no objection to the application to amend the exhibit list, Your Honour. That's the simplest thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can we agree? This one request is granted. So the exhibit list is amended. This is the first step. And now let's go through the documents that were tendered today by the Defence. It would start with D110. And let me see where is the exhibit list. This was 65 ter number 356. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say to shorten matters, there's no objection by the Prosecution to the admission of the exhibits that were put through General Wilmot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Excellent. Then this would be true for D111, D112. I think that's it, Madam Registrar. Correct me if I am wrong, please. So these are in any event admitted into evidence as D110, D111, D112 respectively. Then yesterday, we had already admitted into evidence the report provided by the General and the footnotes. Any problems with the footnotes, first of all, because they have been given numbers today. We have it in a special file. And my question is: Is there any problem related to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, to be frank, we have not had the time to review them. But in the interests of time, we don't object. They can come in. We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, as I outlined in our general rules on the admission of evidence, a decision is subject to any other decision, maybe this may be reversed for unforeseeable reasons. But nevertheless, it stays, this statement with all the footnotes is admitted into evidence. Then, may I please have additional comments by the Defence, what about the additional binders? I think it was seven or so, seven binders, by the expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The Defence, Your Honour, would also move to have those seven binders introduced and admitted into evidence. We have for the Court and for the Office of the Prosecution an outline, if you will, or an index of those documents within the binders if the Court would like and the OTP to review that. Some of them are overlapping with other documents and with the footnotes, but what we've done is we've broken them down from the binders as they existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we haven't -- we do object because, first, we don't know what they are. We were, I understand, provided with them yesterday or the day that the General started testifying. And apparently, they do overlap. We're just going to run into the situation where the footnotes are repeated or the 65 ters are repeated or Prosecution exhibits are repeated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this is why we are somewhat confused, that's because we have been getting documents, the like of which we haven't seen in the last few days. The only bundles of documents that we have received from the Defence are three binders which we went through, the extra documents we got last night which we haven't been through, we have no idea what seven binders Your Honours and Mr. Ostojic are talking about at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admittedly so do I. I only know they are somewhere. I don't know if they are in this courtroom or where they are seven binders. I don't know what it is. I think it's never heard in this courtroom, this way of procedure. I don't know. How can you ask us or request the admission into evidence? As I said previously, normally the judiciary should act blindfolded, but not when it comes to the admission of evidence. So I don't know what we are discussing in the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I could clarify it a little more, Your Honour, and my apologies for that. Each of the documents within the binders are documents received by the Defence from the OTP. As I believe briefly mentioned to the Court, we had all those documents in the B/C/S version and requested their translation. All those documents that are listed in the seven binders are included in our Defence 65 ter list. Of that list we received from the OTP, as I mentioned, the fact that close to 60 to 75 per cent of the documents had been translated for the OTP at a prior time, and there was that reason to retranslate them. The documents we believe are important because General Wilmot clearly relied on those documents, although he doesn't reference each and every document. But also we believe that in the interests of justice, since they are not documents that were generated by anyone in particular but documents that the OTP state clearly that they have seized and produced to us, all with their ERN numbers with the exception of what I believe six books, I believe they are not only relevant but that the Court, in order to get closer to the truth and to determine exactly what may have occurred, should look at those documents as well as the testimony of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I, before I give the floor to the Prosecution once again, ask General Wilmot: Is this a compilation of yours or a compilation provided by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's a compilation of mine. Of course, I got some assistance from them because I didn't know where the documents were. And I haven't -- a lot of the documents I simply scanned and didn't read in their totality, but I was searching for ideas, thoughts, the flow of activity and so forth, and that's how we got to this series of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So one could regard it as the basic documents for your report and you relying on these documents at least in part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Essentially that's true, sir. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I recall that whenever a decision is made, it is possible to reverse the decision, but as to the fact that at this moment, General Wilmot, the expert, has stated that it is his own compilation and the basis for his statement, can I invite the Prosecution that we admit this into evidence today, and of course subject to any other decision and also under the - we discussed it briefly during the break - under all reservations by the Trial Chamber, that in case we identify some documents not related to our case or where there are any other obstacles under the rules to admit these documents into evidence, that document by document a reverse decision can be made?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could we proceed this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We could if Your Honour actually prefers that and we want to accommodate the Court, the Court staff, and the Defence. But what I understand from what Mr. Ostojic just said, all these documents are on the Defence 65 ter list. It makes much more sense when we have a list and numbers to use that list rather than duplicate and admit seven bundles that apparently are duplicative of either Prosecution exhibits or Defence 65 ter list exhibits. I think we're all going to be extremely confused if we do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We did compile a list of the binders reflecting the 65 ter number, column for the date of the document as it appears on the document, the source, and the title, and the brief description, and we state the volume and section that it can be found within the seven binders. We would be happy to pass that out as we suggested earlier to the OTP, to the Court, and to your staff. If we need to make a reservation like that, we don't object, we just believe that it is necessary to get a complete picture, as we've stated. We understand that it is an irregular way of doing things, and we certainly apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it true that all the documents included in these seven binders are already either exhibits by the Prosecution, by the Defence, or by the Judges? No additional document included?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. That would not be accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So there would be additional documents included not yet admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Ostojic said that they were all on the 65 ter list, not yet admitted but on that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On the 65 ter list. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the amended motion that the Court just granted because we have the documents that appear on Mr. Butler's report but are not attached to his report, namely the military documents that we in part referenced today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But if this is the case, that all documents are already delivered, put it this way, under 65 ter, and you have a compilation, and the list of these documents, then I can't see any reason why we would have to copy this -- I think it would be necessary to copy these seven binders 12 times. And I think we should protect the forest. And therefore it's more than reasonable that we limit ourselves to these lists. And my suggestion would be to admit only this list that we have an overview what is in these seven binders. And these seven binders should be available only once and in the Registry. The transcript has --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Realtime transcript read in error "MR. KOUMJIAN:"] May I suggest, as Your Honour rightly said, that at the moment we just admit the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The LiveNote has frozen. Under the -- yes. Under the impression that -- we can move on. It works again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think I'm Mr. Koumjian -- although I agree it's very difficulty. Your Honour, we only admit the list, allow us over the weekend to look at what's on the list. May I say this, we do have an objection in principle to certain documents. And that is extracts from books taken out of context which nobody has explained the relevance at all in particular, in respect of the evidence given by Dr. Trifkovic, the first four -- sorry, six exhibits on their list are extracts from books. Number 2, there's no translation at all. That's who defended Bosnia. Number 4 deals with events in Sanski Most. And Your Honour, in principle, we do object to these extracts taken from books, taken out of context completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I briefly reply. I believe my learned friend is looking at a list filed on the 18th of November, 2002, our 65 ter list. We've tendered to the Court a list of the documents within the seven binders, so not to confuse the two and so what we tendered to the Court and what we are asking to be moved into evidence right now are the seven binders that General Wilmot relied on which was essentially, among other things, daily military reports from the 1st Krajina, 5th Kozara, and 43rd Motorised Brigade which we believe are consistent with the testimony that the Court heard and will enlighten us on further facts within that testimony and from those statements and other documents. With respect to Ms. Korner's comments on the 65 ter motion and those six books, we can hopefully resolve that this evening once we meet. I don't know that the books are necessarily critical. We have not at this point moved to include those books as evidence, so I think the point might be moot at least at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's I'm really confused now. On the new list we have been given, those books appear on the last page. Items 1 through to 6. That's why I say, I'm really now totally and utterly confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To be very pragmatic, can it do any harm or create any prejudice for any of us if they admit only this new list as such, and this doesn't say anything about the documents included in this list? And this would give us access to the basic materials of General Wilmot, and whoever wants can go to the Registry, find these documents compiled in these seven files. And I think this avoids this unnecessary copying of all these documents we have already another time. Can the parties agree with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sure we'll be able to work it out, Your Honour. Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, admission of the list absolutely no objection, as I said. Admission of the documents on the list into evidence is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar, correct me please if I'm wrong, this list would be J113 -- D113. Correct? Okay. Then this is admitted into evidence as D113A, because it's only in English. Are there any other documents related to our current expert witness, General Wilmot, that we have to discuss in his presence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Apparently this is not the case. There are no further questions. I have to thank you for your expertise, for your clear answers. We have to see how we assess your expertise. And as the body of the United Nations, I do not hesitate if I say that even those comments you made today not relevant for this case are very much appreciated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very kindly, sir, and thank you for your hospitality I'll call it and many politenesses. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I wish you a safe trip home, especially under the prevailing circumstances. May I ask the usher to escort the now-excused witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then, it remains for us to discuss hopefully without any additional confusion the remaining documents. And this would be the aforementioned documents tendered by the Defence. What is now -- this is another question. The documents 249 through 650, I asked the parties since November last year whether they came to an agreement on the admission of evidence, because the Trial Chamber would be prepared to accept a package solution, save there would be any objections by the Prosecution. And if I understood it correctly, there were only some minor documents to be discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not I'm afraid quite as simple as that. We've only gone through documents 1 to 249. 250 to 650 effectively, we think we got last night, with the translations. So we haven't looked at any of those. I can see Mr. Ostojic is shaking his head, so if he tells us we've had them before. So all we can deal with today, and it's really a matter of principle which may assist, is the ones we've looked at, which is 1 through 249.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think this is fair enough, and we ourselves would have made the reservation that we are not in a situation where we could decide responsibly and conscientiously on documents we haven't seen before. We received these other documents this morning, as outlined beforehand. I learned from Madam Registrar that we need to have a short break. So therefore, the trial stays adjourned until 5 minutes past 4.00 that we can go through the remaining documents. And may I ask Madam Registrar to provide the parties with the document "problematic documents" that we can discuss it in this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Let's turn to the problematic documents in the order. S151A, what about the translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm so sorry. I'm obviously a bit confused at the moment. We have -- I understand we have an English transcript of this, although the video itself is in B/C/S. And Your Honour wants what, a B/C/S transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have to go back to the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: A new English version, that's what is needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You want a new English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it was only a rough translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told somebody's working on it. It's more or less ready and it should be available next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then S368.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Defence was to specify which part of the electronic database they want accessed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's on the list of missing persons from the database Nastradali. May I ask the Defence, is this problem settled?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's my understanding that it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then this part in the exhibit list can be redacted, this comment. S393.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it has been submitted for translation to CLSS. We're just checking to see whether we've had the translation back. As yet, we don't think we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The problem here was that it was not admitted for now because it was not legible. And then the next step was to provide an original. If my recollection serves me correctly, we sought -- we reviewed this document and found out that it was not possible for the translation -- to have a proper translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I've got the original from the vault and actually brought it into the courtroom and asked one of the interpreters in one of the booths to see whether they were able to distinguish it so that we could put it on the ELMO and then we would be able to read it. But they said in fact that they -- it was illegible for them. So then we were going to submit it through the official channel to the CLSS to try and get them to see if it could be translated. And so we're just waiting to see whether it comes back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, that we're only clear what the problem is with this. If it's not legible, then it's not legible. We had ourselves especially with the assistance of Judge Vassylenko ourselves problems to read this. So please let us know in the course of the next week whether there is a translation possible or not. D55.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was the statute, and Mr. Corin is hopeful to deliver some kind of report next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: During rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: During rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then an extremely confusing matter once again, the exhibits tendered by Mr. Trifkovic. Unfortunately, I wasn't present during the entire testimony, so therefore it's more or less hearsay or reading the transcript. But the parties were to come together and determine which documents are undisputed and therefore ripe for admission. And then to find out where there's no agreement or no translation in order that the Chamber could rule on these documents. And the idea was to have this admitted as D92, and then in our customary way, add a dash, and then add document by document. May I ask the Prosecution, was there a possibility to go these three binders until now and do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is what I have been sort of going back to for the last half hour. These are the documents 1 to 249. Those are the ones that the three of us had gone through. I dealt with the first volume, which for the majority, there is no objection. And it would be easier I think if I indicate the ones to which there is an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Excellent. Let's proceed this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I go back to what I said earlier, which is the question of these books. And, Your Honour, I go back to 1 to 249 which are on the list of the 18th of November, which I think is really the only list we ever had until now. Your Honours, 1 through until 6 are sections of various books which allegedly Dr. Trifkovic looked at. He did not refer to any of the page numbers except in one or two cases, I think. But what has been put in are sections from these books. Book number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You refer to "Chaos, Some Chaos. Chaos, Some Chaos." These books --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Items 1, the first is Bosnian warriors, but a man called Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: These books appearing now as 1 to 6, following 522 on the list we received --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's -- simply the logic of this escapes me completely, but it's now on the last page after 522. You will see items 1 to 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And it's not without cynicism that the first article reads "some chaos."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely. So, Your Honour, our objection is to that. They have never really been dealt with, either by anybody referring Your Honours to the pages. They are parts of this book. We don't know whether they are representative of the whole book or not. May I point out, I don't know who did it, but in book number 1, "The Bosnian Warriors," the copy we have been given has got underlining in the original text which has been repeated in the translation, so it does go. I think we ought to have clean copies go in. For book number 2, "Who Defended Bosnia," no translation has been provided to us. Book number 4 deals with events in Sanski Most, and Your Honours ruled on a number of occasion that we shouldn't put in documents that dealt with municipalities outside of Prijedor. And, Your Honour, the -- when I say "books 1 to 6," I would slightly withdraw that of number 5. It's the book by Mr. Sivac. But again, it's only partial. But principally, we would object to parts of books going in which haven't been dealt with by witnesses properly in evidence and without witnesses pointing out what they say the relevance of those books are. Your Honour, shall I deal with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I would just add that during the break, the Judges briefly deliberated on this issue, and the objections - your objections - our objections have in common that it's indeed in part out of context and normally, one can read a book, a law, or whatsoever only in context. And in part, the translation is not provided. And in addition, we have reasonable doubts whether this is really necessary, a question of -- let alone the question of relevance at this point in time. Therefore, I would ask the Defence, is it really necessary to make -- to request the admission into evidence of these books? Because then it might be that we would have to ask for the entire book in a language we understand. And isn't it in fact enough that we have admitted into evidence Trifkovic's expertise relying on this, and thereby incorporating this into his expert report? Therefore, may I ask you, are you prepared to withdraw this request related to the excerpts of these six books?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, if I may clarify for the Court, we were advised by the translation department, and I believe your office, that we should submit only the portions of the book that we felt were relevant to be translated in light of the amount of documents that the department has to translate. That's why we selected certain portions of the book. Quite frankly, I think each of the books should be introduced into evidence because they offer a perspective which I think would assist the Court in coming closer to the truth and would protect the interests of justice in this trial. Secondly, or third, each of these books seems to be an account of first-hand information which we believe is reliable, and therefore necessary in order to get a clear picture. My next, I believe, opinion and basis for asking that the books be introduced into evidence, specifically book number 6, who's author is Mr. Sefer Halilovic, the Court will recall that we had multiple discussions relating to Mr. Halilovic including the possibility of the Office of the Prosecution giving us the statements that he has given to him -- to them them as well as with the possibility of having Mr. Halilovic testify in this case. I think it's necessary to keep things in context that we did not obtain Mr. Halilovic's exhaustive interviews with the OTP, but we know that obviously he's indicted, and we would like that book to be introduced into evidence so that there's no dispute, unless there can be an agreement as to when the Patriotic League was formed, when the Green Berets were formed, and when if indeed the mujahedin were actually in the Prijedor and the Bosnia area. We believe that book being a first-hand account has been translated. We are speculating on that, but we can't imagine that the Office of the Prosecution, while indicting an individual such as Mr. Halilovic, does not have that book in its entirety translated and has used it as some sort of basis for evidence that soon will come forth against that individual in his upcoming trial. We will attempt if the Court wishes to have the entire books translated. We submitted only the portions of the book that we felt were relevant, and we believe that the books should be introduced into evidence for those reasons, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the Prosecution related to the last book only by Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know is the answer to that, whether we've ever had it translated. The persons who are dealing with that prosecution -- I don't know the answer -- no. I mean, it's a different team. That's what I'm trying to say, and I don't know the answer but I could make a check. Your Honour, it doesn't negate the point that I'm making, which is that to put parts of that book in, possibly out of context, without anybody explaining why it is relevant, Your Honour, in our submission, is not a suitable basis for admission. But Your Honour, I will make a check on whether we have a translation in-house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I think the arguments have been exchanged, and we have to rule on these six books especially, and I think, yes, this was one special problem only. Then may I take it from your statement that there are no other documents in the three files or -- if not, please let me know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I was going to deal with, as I say, we each dealt with a separate binder, and I know that in the binders 2 and 3, there are more documents which seem to have no relevance at all. Between documents 1 to 89, which is what I looked at, Your Honour, I don't know whether Your Honour wants me to indicate to you, but a number of them are already Prosecution exhibits, and I have a couple of queries of relevance in respect of Document Number 16 -- perhaps if I just indicate the numbers, then Your Honours can look at it. Your Honours, sorry, Documents number 11, 16, and 42, 46, 55, and 56. And that is it. But Your Honours, Documents 7; 12; 14; 17 to 19 inclusive; 22 and 23; and 37; 64; and 73; and 82 are all already Prosecution exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So therefore, the request by the Defence becomes moot related to these documents. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If Prosecution could be so kind related to all the three binders to give Madam Registrar the numbers you find out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, finally simply this: On 26, we never got a document at all. Actually I think that was an oversight in the bundles. And for number 37, there's no translation. And, Your Honour, on the first set those are the only remarks that I have. Mr. Koumjian dealt with the second set, and Ms. Sutherland the third.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's proceed, please, this way, that you announce where you have objections based on relevance, and then on the second part, those documents which are already admitted into evidence. So, Mr. Koumjian, as I understand, responsible for file number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may interrupt just before Mr. Koumjian, did counsel say 37 they do not have a translation? Because I believe she also said 37 is a Prosecution exhibit, so -- just so that we're clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, you're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Microphone, Ms. Korner, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in this binder, there are a great number of documents which while we can't say that they prejudice us, we see no relevance and no value. They generally refer to events that took place outside of Prijedor. But before I go into those, there are a few we seem to be missing. And that would be the 65 ter number 146 and 147, we don't see any -- in my binder, I didn't see any document under those numbers. Under 174 and 175, there was no translation. And 180, we also were missing the document. The documents that I did not see any relevance to the events in Prijedor were numbers 104 - it's actually a very long list - 106; 109 through 115, all of those; 118; 119; 121; 123 through 126, all four of those; 130 through 134, those five documents; 136; 139; 141; 143; 148; 151; 153; 158; 161; 164; 170; 172; 173; 177; 179; 181; 182; 183; 188; 189; and 193.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I can only say we will rule on this as soon as practicable. Then file 3, please, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the same goes for this binder in relation to what Mr. Koumjian said, his opening remarks on binder 2. utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be, because I don't know whether we have all the same binders, starting with -- you say irrelevant from your point of view is Document --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, Your Honour. I wasn't clear. I've got the binder Rule 65 ter numbers 200 to 249. The three documents that I think are relevant for Prijedor are 201, 222, 228.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is what I understood. I only wanted to know where you started. 200, correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any documents already admitted into evidence amongst those?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. There are some other documents that are relevant generally, and that is in relation to Rule 65 ter number 200, there are in fact four articles in that one number, so it's the article with the title "Concern About BH."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The next one is 206 and 207, 208, 209. 211 is, in fact, Exhibit D77. 214, 223, 224. 225 is, in fact, D78. 226, query; possibly 227; 231; 232; 233; 237; 238; 239. utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, you mentioned previously you regard as relevant 201, 222, 228 --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: They go specifically dealing with events in the Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then those you just listed, you regard as absolutely irrelevant or --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm saying they are generally relevant. We don't object to them being admitted. They don't specifically mention the Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this distinction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Also 241 and 245. I'm sorry, I missed those two. No, I'm sorry, Your Honour. 241 and 245 are in another pile of documents. And that is the three other articles in Rule 65 ter number 200. Then the following: 202, 203, 204, 205, 210, 212, 213, 215, 216, 217, 218, 219, 221, 229, 230, 234, 236, 241, 243, 244, 245, 246, 247, 249. And that completes the third binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned 225 twice. Once on page 39, line 9, and then again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, Your Honour, that's because it deals with refugees and it's also --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Ms. Sutherland, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes. Yes, because it's already an exhibit, I withdraw the fact that I said just a moment ago that because it was dealing with refugees it's irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Also here, the Chamber will rule as soon as practical because I think the Defence will stick to their submission that these documents are relevant without any doubt. And then the next question was -- could we go for a moment in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Related to Document S419, what about the biography of the author Mirko Pejanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I did actually provide to the Defence the whole book to take a photocopy of the other day. But I haven't as yet made arrangements for the -- his biography as -- but I will do that so Your Honours can have it on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the other documents given by Mr. Trifkovic spontaneously, the 19th of March, 2003. Is it necessary? Does the Defence tender this document, which is only part of the document, public domain, accessible on the Internet?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It would be our position, Your Honour, that in order to keep a complete record, that the documents do be introduced in as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So then the single page -- sorry, I forgot the right to be heard by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't object to it. I would rather have liked to have seen the second article as well. But, Your Honour, as far as I'm concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Step by step. So the first -- the only one page, once again, only part of an entire document therefore admitted into evidence as D114. Correct, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The article by Alfred Rubin, what about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, again, Your Honour, there are -- I do have some reservations, but I'm not prepared to put them forward strongly. I do think, however, it would be better if we saw a second article that he said was conjoined to produce the composite. But as I say, I don't feel strongly enough to pursue that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence, D115. The third, I think it's settled. Then none of the parties tendered the sample of U.S. commentary on the witness's work on Islam. I think this is really superfluous. We don't need this. But of course, it's for the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it is superfluous, Your Honour, but it is in order to keep a complete record, we could just formally tender. But for whatever it's worth and I think in the transcript it's referred to, so just if anyone goes back to review it, they would know what it is that they are referencing. But we are not really moving one way or the other in connection with that document, but formally I guess we are moving it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, well it's slightly different because he merely volunteered that he had them, and nobody looked into them and nobody asked a single question. So I don't see how that takes as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Absolutely. Not admitted into evidence. Madam Registrar, that's all? Any problems from your side, from your perspective in the moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just ask Your Honour -- I know we are slightly over but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, no, no. We are not -- let's continue, nothing with exhibits. So therefore, before closing the Defence case, I have once again to ask the Defence: Is there any intention to call Dr. Stakic as a witness, or does Dr. Stakic want to give a statement under Rule 84 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence would ask respectfully that it may close its case on Monday. We have not, under the time constraints with the issues, been able to fully and in my opinion completely resolve that issue. If the Court presses us to close the case today, we will do so respectfully. Then the answer to the question will be that Dr. Stakic will not give a statement pursuant to the rules as they are envisioned. However, if we would be given an opportunity just to clarify any and all issues, to determine clearly that that is the case, we would ask that we close the case formally on Monday of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There is no obstacle to reopen the case if your client decides to make use of his right enshrined especially in Rule 84 bis. Anything else? Any motion during the Defence case?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's just something Your Honour raised, I think it was on Monday of this week that I want to discuss. But I'd like to do that in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It has to do with the Defence case?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It has to do -- well, I'm not sure what it has to do. I think it's Your Honours' calling of witnesses it has to do with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That's the next step.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask formally the Defence, are there any other motions or any other evidence under Rule 85(ii)?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence would just like to remind the Court respectfully that when reviewing the objections as to relevance to the documents that we submit, that they specifically focus on paragraphs 26 and 27, although we're unclear as to how facts as cited in the indictment relating as far back as 1991 and allegations with respect to joint criminal enterprise as set forth in those two paragraphs of the fourth amended count, how the Prosecution can now claim that articles contemporaneous with the events as they have alleged should or are not relevant. So we would just respectfully have the Court and direct your attention to that. Other than that, we have no other comments at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And no other motions, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear the Court, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No other motions, no other evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. The Defence will formally rest its case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. This then concludes the Defence case under Rule 85(A)(ii). Then we have to turn to the events of next week hopefully to take place. Once again, step by step. I raise the question whether or not during rebuttal, Prosecution intends to call Mr. Dosen, being now available as a witness, during rebuttal?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's what I was about to deal with, and could I ask that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the Defence, do they have -- do you have already an opinion on the 92 bis transcripts?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, we do have an opinion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's a preliminary opinion, Your Honour, but quite frankly as I understand the Rules of Evidence in this Tribunal, the OTP had an allegation in connection with specifically the town of Ljubija. They apparently have called some witnesses, although now they themselves view it as not enough witnesses, to establish a prima facie case both as to widespread and systematic and as to whether crimes occurred in the town of Ljubija. The Court unfortunately, either pursuant to our motion or proprio motu, did not dismiss during the 98 bis portion of this case the entirety of Ljubija and felt that there was enough evidence in connection with that for the Prosecution. The Defence, trying to meet its obligation, brought witnesses from that town in order to rebut, contradict, and refute the allegations set forth in the fourth amended complaint -- or the fourth amended indictment alleging that specific town. My understanding of rebuttal is to rebut new evidence, not to rehash and reopen their case to add evidence which would assist them because they either failed, respectfully, or neglected to bring forth such evidence. They are not rebutting our witnesses, they are merely adding witnesses to support their initial claim. We still believe that that entire portion should have been dismissed pursuant to 98. We respect the Court's ruling on that. We brought witnesses to rebut that. Now to give them an opportunity to add witnesses in that case would in essence be reopening their case so that they can call witnesses on those issues. We think it is highly inappropriate. It is not a new issue. Therefore, there is nothing to rebut. Rebuttal and rejoinder are for only issues that have arisen that were not covered. This is an allegation that goes to many elements and factors that are in the fourth amended indictment that we have already addressed. So we think it's appropriate for both witnesses, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I didn't want to discuss the prerequisites of 92 bis lengthy today. The only question was in case the Trial Chamber comes to the conclusion that it is admissable on -- during rebuttal under 92 bis, would there be a request for cross-examination of these witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I thought you wanted my general opinion on the issue. Yes, of course the Defence wants to cross-examine these witnesses, and we think it's most important in light of the fact that we brought witnesses which we believe were credible and showed the events which were contradictory to those which they are not supporting. So yes, we would be asking formally to cross-examine those witnesses pursuant to 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clear statement, because it's now to coordinate the next weeks and to see what is necessary, what time we will need. All the other issues related to the prerequisites and especially the 94 bis admission of an expert report already once rejected by the Chamber, this we can discuss, no doubt, on Tuesday. On Wednesday we start hopefully with the examination, let's call it the examination-in-chief by the Judges, of Mr. Kuruzovic. Any comments on this in the moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Your Honour knows the submissions we've made on it, so I anticipate that Your Honours will be giving a warning. But the only other matter is whether Mr. Kuruzovic should have with him a lawyer to represent him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have already taken this into account, and there would be a standby counsel ready if need may be. I take it from the statement, from the previous statement, that Mr. Kuruzovic was prepared to testify without the assistance of counsel. But under this special, extremely special circumstances, as I said previously, a suspect appearing as a witness, but not indicted, I think it's only fair that if the person so wishes, counsel be present. So if we are in agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then on Thursday, as to the fact there was an overlapping of a long Status Conference in another case, we switched with the Galic case. And therefore, the hearing, the second day of the hearing of Mr. Kuruzovic, will take place in the morning of Thursday next week. If need may be, and it's really not foreseeable how long this witness will take us, may I ask the parties - I already addressed this issue early this morning - would the parties be prepared to continue Friday, 28? Please, you maybe have the most important problems at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The parties will be prepared to proceed on Monday with the continued cross-examination of Mr. Kuruzovic. I would just ask the Court respectfully that the Court reconsiders our request orally in connection with the written briefs to be submitted, because the time frame is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I asked for Friday, and you answered related to Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We are prepared to proceed on next Friday, Your Honour, and if necessary, the following Monday as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. What about Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We're quite prepared, Your Honour.

utterances.text: So this would take place in Courtroom I, Madam Registrar, correct? We have just received a new courtroom calendar. We have to decide later in which courtroom we will continue on Friday. So for the moment, the next difficult week seems to be relatively clear. Any other urgent submissions for today? The Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. This concludes today's and this weeks' hearing. And we continue in the same courtroom. Therefore we may leave some of the documents here in this courtroom. Monday 9.00. The trial stays adjourned until Monday, 9.00.
